validate that their customizations, third-party integrations and data flows work
correctly before production cutover. No customer data from other customers is
accessible in preview environments; each preview environment is logically isolated
with separate databases and caches.

Preview environments run on shared infrastructure and have no SLA guarantees,
meaning planned downtime is possible with less than seventy-two hours notice. Preview
environments receive the same automatic security updates as production but may be
rebooted without warning for infrastructure maintenance. Preview environments use
the same multi-tenant architecture as production, so customers test with complete
isolation but realistic system behavior. Data in preview environments is completely
segregated from production data; no customer preview data can leak into production
or into other customers' preview environments.

The rule governing all customer use of release candidates is absolute and non-
negotiable: no customer runs release 15.0.0-rc3 in production without signed
preview agreement on file. The preview agreement is a legal contract clarifying that
Northwind provides best-effort support during preview period but does not guarantee
uptime, performance, or stability, and that customer accepts full risk of running
pre-release software in production context. Customers who deploy preview releases
into production without signed agreement are not eligible for SLA credits, penalty
fees or service credits if the release candidate causes incidents or data loss. This
policy protects both parties by establishing clear expectations and liability
boundaries before preview deployment. Some customers who previously ran release
candidates without agreements have requested to formalize them retroactively; all
such requests are declined and customers are required to downgrade to a stable
release immediately.

The preview agreement is valid for ninety days from signature and must be renewed
for each subsequent release candidate before deployment. Nadia Petrov's support team
coordinates the preview agreement process and can typically turn around completed,
legal-reviewed agreement within two to three business days from request. Customers
interested in preview access should contact their account team or email
support@northwind.example for preview agreement paperwork and preview environment
provisioning.

The support team can also arrange training sessions on 15.0.0-rc3 features and
migration planning, covering multi-region deployment strategies, query optimizer
usage, and anomaly detection configuration. Training sessions last two hours and
include hands-on exercises with sample data. Customers should plan migration
testing for multi-region features well in advance, as the feature requires
changes to connection string configuration and data replication setup. The
migration guide covers both active-passive and active-active topologies with
specific configuration examples for each.

Customers who participated in preview cycles for 15.0.0-rc1 and 15.0.0-rc2 have
provided feedback on the multi-region feature's usability and performance
characteristics. Most feedback was positive, though some customers requested the
ability to configure per-region rate limits independently. This feature is
planned for 15.1 and not available in 15.0.0-rc3. Early adopters should expect
the general availability release on August 15, 2026 to be production-ready with
no additional significant changes beyond bug fixes since rc3.

title: On-Call Rotation
body:
# On-Call Rotation

## Purpose

The on-call rotation provides 24/7 coverage for incidents at Northwind
Systems. On-call engineers respond to SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents (see
the Incident Escalation Matrix) and to P0 and P1 support tickets (see
the Support SLA Policy), outside and inside business hours. The
rotation is owned by engineering and is open to engineers at L3 and
above who have completed the on-call training. This policy is public
because support and operations work with the rotation daily. The
on-call calendar is published on the engineering calendar and in the
operations portal, and every engineer can see who is on call at any
time.

## Rotation Structure

The rotation is weekly: an engineer is on primary call for one week,
from Wednesday 10:00 CT to the following Wednesday 10:00 CT. The
handoff is Wednesday 10:00 CT, with a 30-minute handoff meeting
between the outgoing and incoming engineers, covering open incidents,
known issues, and the state of the environment. Every primary slot
has a backup on-call engineer, who covers when the primary is
unavailable or is already engaged on an incident. No engineer is
primary more than one week in four, and no engineer is primary in two
consecutive weeks. The schedule is built three months in advance, and
swaps are managed in the on-call calendar with manager approval.

## Response Requirements

The primary on-call engineer acknowledges pages within 5 minutes and
responds within 15 minutes for SEV-1, and within 30 minutes for
SEV-2, around the clock. The backup responds if the primary does not
acknowledge within 10 minutes. The response standard is the same on
weekends and holidays; holiday coverage follows the Channel and Hours
Policy's holiday rules. On-call engineers must be able to reach a
computer with production access within 30 minutes of a SEV-1 page;
being at a location without connectivity is declared in the on-call
calendar in advance. The incident response itself follows the
Incident Escalation Matrix: the on-call engineer decides severity,
and the on-call lead (a manager or director on the same rotation)
acts as incident commander for SEV-1 and SEV-2.

## On-Call Pay and Time Off

On-call engineers receive a stipend of $150 per day on call, paid
monthly with the normal payroll. Hours actually worked during an
incident are compensated as time off in lieu: one hour of time off
per hour worked on an incident, banked and usable within 90 days,
per the Leave and Time Off Policy's manager approval rules. A SEV-1
incident that runs more than 4 hours past midnight grants the
engineer the following business day off automatically, arranged with
the manager. On-call duty does not change the Remote Work and
Flexible Hours Policy: the on-call week is still a normal working
week, and the stipend is compensation for the availability, not for
hours.

## Escalation Chain

If the primary cannot resolve or the severity warrants it, the
escalation chain is: primary, backup, on-call lead (incident
commander), the CTO, then the CEO for SEV-1 incidents past the
4-hour mark. The support manager is on the chain for customer-facing
incidents, and the CISO joins for security incidents. The chain is
published in the on-call calendar with contact details, and the
Channel and Hours Policy's out-of-hours escalation path (on-call
engineer, support manager on call, VP of Support) runs in parallel
for customer communication. Escalation decisions are logged in the
incident record (INC-####).

## Readiness and Training

Engineers join the rotation after completing: the on-call training
(incident response, communication, the escalation matrix), a
shadow week with a primary, and a supervised first week. The
engineering manager tracks readiness and can pull an engineer from
the rotation if their incident response reviews show gaps. The
on-call training is refreshed annually, in line with the security
awareness training in the Regulatory Compliance Calendar. The
rotation includes engineers from all product teams, so the on-call
engineer for a service is always backed by the owning team's manager
via the escalation chain; the owning team is on the calendar too.

## Metrics and Review

The on-call metrics are reviewed monthly by the engineering manager:
page-to-acknowledge time, page-to-response time, incidents per week,
and stipend spend. The targets: 95% of pages acknowledged within 5
minutes, and 95% of SEV-1 responses within 15 minutes. Missed pages
are reviewed in the weekly engineering meeting, and repeated misses
are handled by the manager. The on-call stipend budget is part of the
engineering budget in the Budget Planning and Forecasting cycle.
The on-call calendar is archived at the end of each year and retained
for three years under the System Log Retention Policy's operational
records.

title: Security and Vulnerability Policy
sourceName: Northwind Engineering Security and Vulnerability Policy
body:
# Security and Vulnerability Policy

## Purpose and Audience

This policy defines how Northwind Systems manages security: access
controls, vulnerability handling, patching, and the security review
process. It is written for directors and IT administrators, who own
the controls; it is the internal security policy and is not shared
with customers. The customer-facing summary of our security posture
lives in the Privacy Policy and the marketing trust page. The policy
is owned by the CISO, Priya Raman, and the CTO. Questions go to
security@northwind.example. The Incident Escalation Matrix covers
incident response; this policy covers prevention and remediation.

## Access Control

Access is granted on a need-to-know basis, through the access request
process: the requester's manager approves, and the IT admin grants
the minimum access for the role. Access is reviewed quarterly by
managers against the access list, and revoked within 24 hours of a
role change or departure (see the Termination and Offboarding
Policy). Privileged access (production, admin consoles, security
logs) requires: a separate approval from the CISO's team, MFA on
every privileged account, and session logging. Shared accounts are
prohibited. API keys follow the API and Integration Standards: scoped
to minimum permissions, rotated at least every 90 days, and revoked
on offboarding. Access review findings are logged and retained for
three years.

## Vulnerability Management

Vulnerabilities are tracked with a severity rating: critical, high,
medium, and low. The patch schedule: critical vulnerabilities are
patched within 7 days, high within 30 days, medium within 90 days,
and low at the next scheduled maintenance. Patching applies to
production systems, customer-facing services, and internal tools
alike; the CI pipeline scans dependencies on every build and blocks
merges on critical or high findings. A critical vulnerability with no
available patch is mitigated with compensating controls (network
isolation, access restriction) and reported to the CTO. The
vulnerability register is reviewed weekly by the CISO's team, and
patch compliance is reported monthly to the CTO.

## Security Review in Development

Every pull request is checked against the security checklist in the
Software Development Lifecycle: input validation, authentication and
authorization, injection resistance, secrets handling, and logging
of security events. Changes touching authentication, payment, or
data export are reviewed by a security reviewer (a member of the
CISO's team) in addition to the two standard approvals. Security
review findings block the merge. The checklist is updated annually
and after every SEV-1 or SEV-2 security incident. Security training
for engineers runs annually in March (per the Regulatory Compliance
Calendar), and engineers who work on authentication or payment
systems complete an additional module.

## Security Incidents

A security incident is any confirmed or suspected compromise of
confidentiality, integrity, or availability involving Northwind
systems or data. Security incidents are classified under the
Incident Escalation Matrix: SEV-1 for confirmed breaches with
impact, SEV-2 for suspected breaches under investigation. The CISO
leads the security response, and the incident record (INC-####)
captures the timeline. Breach notification follows the Privacy
Policy: reportable breaches are notified to affected customers
within 72 hours of confirmation, and to authorities where local law
requires. Postmortems for security incidents include the root cause,
the remediation, and the control changes, and are approved by the
CISO. Security incident records are retained for seven years per the
System Log Retention Policy.

## Responsible Disclosure

Northwind operates a responsible disclosure program for external
researchers. Reports go to security@northwind.example and are
acknowledged within 5 business days. The disclosure timeline: Northwind
commits to fix confirmed critical and high findings within the patch
schedule (7 and 30 days) and to public disclosure within 90 days of
the fix, coordinated with the researcher. The program scope is the
public products and the developer portal; out-of-scope targets are
listed on the disclosure page. The CISO decides whether a finding is
in scope and whether it is eligible for public acknowledgment.
Researchers who follow the program's rules are not pursued
legally; researchers who do not are handled under the IP and
Confidentiality Policy's breach process.

## Compliance Controls

The security controls in this policy are audited twice a year in the
SOC 2 Type II audits (April and October fieldwork, per the Regulatory
Compliance Calendar) and every three years in the ISO 27001
recertification. The audit evidence includes: the access review
logs, the vulnerability register, the patch compliance report, and
the incident records. The CISO reports security metrics to the board
at the May board meeting per the Board Reporting Calendar. Security
control changes are logged in the change system (CHG-####) under the
Change Management Policy. Violations of this policy by employees are
handled under the Termination and Offboarding Policy, and violations
by contractors terminate the engagement under the Contractor Expense
Policy's breach rules.

title: Software Development Lifecycle
body:
# Software Development Lifecycle

## Purpose

This policy defines how software is built at Northwind Systems: from
idea to production. It covers planning, development, testing, review,
and release, and it applies to every product (Northwind Core, Atlas,
Meridian) and to internal tooling. It is an engineering policy, and
it is shared only within engineering because it contains internal
quality targets and review rules. The CTO owns the lifecycle, and the
engineering manager for each team runs it. The Code Deployment
Policy covers the deployment mechanics, and the Change Management
Policy covers the production change process; this policy covers what
happens before deployment.

## Planning and Estimation

Work is planned in sprints of two weeks. Every piece of work has a
ticket in the tracker with a size estimate (S, M, L, XL), and work
larger than XL is split before it enters a sprint. Each sprint starts
with planning on Monday and ends with a review and retrospective on
the second Friday. Features follow the roadmap, which the CTO reviews
quarterly; bugs and incidents (SEV-3 and SEV-4) are triaged into
sprints by the engineering manager. Work that is not in the tracker
is not worked on during the sprint, except for incidents and
emergency changes under the Change Management Policy. The roadmap is
confidential per the IP and Confidentiality Policy and is not shared
outside engineering without the CTO's approval.

## Development and Code Review

Code lives in the main branch, and all work happens on short-lived
feature branches. Every change is a pull request with: a description
of the change, the ticket reference, test coverage for changed code,
and a changelog entry. Pull requests require two approvals: one from
a peer and one from the owning engineering manager or director (the
same approval chain as the Code Deployment Policy). No pull request
is merged with unresolved review comments. The review checks:
correctness, test quality, security (using the security checklist in
the Security and Vulnerability Policy), and performance. Code review
turnaround target is one business day; reviews waiting more than two
business days are escalated to the engineering manager.

## Testing Requirements

Test coverage of 80% is required on changed code, enforced by the CI
pipeline. The test suite runs on every pull request: unit tests,
integration tests, and the contract tests for APIs (see the API and
Integration Standards). Critical paths (authentication, billing,
data export) require integration tests in addition to unit tests.
Performance tests run for changes to hot paths, and the results are
reviewed by the engineering manager. Test flakiness is treated as a
bug: a test that fails intermittently is fixed or quarantined within
one sprint, and quarantined tests are tracked. The CI pipeline blocks
merges on test failure, coverage failure, or dependency scan findings.

## Releases and Cadence

Releases ship on the change windows in the Change Management Policy:
Tuesday and Thursday, 10:00 to 14:00 CT, with the annual freeze from
December 15 to January 5. The release cadence is: Core ships every
two weeks, Atlas every month, Meridian every two weeks; hotfixes
ship as emergency changes under the Code Deployment Policy. Each
release has a release owner (the engineering manager of the owning
team), a release notes entry, and a rollback plan. Releases follow
the canary pattern (10% for 30 minutes) in the Code Deployment
Policy. A release that rolls back is reviewed within 5 business
days, and the review findings feed the next sprint's planning.

## Quality Metrics

The quality metrics are reviewed monthly by the engineering manager:
rollback rate (target under 5%), canary failure rate (under 5%),
SEV-2 and above incidents per month, open bug count by severity, and
time to fix for P0 and P1 bugs (the Support SLA Policy's resolution
targets apply to the support side; engineering's fix target is 4
hours for P0 and 24 hours for P1, matching the incident targets).
The metrics feed the monthly engineering report to the CTO and the
April and October SOC 2 audit evidence. A team with two SEV-2
incidents in a quarter gets a process review led by the CTO.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Code Deployment Policy governs deployment mechanics and
approvals. The Change Management Policy governs windows, the freeze,
and the CAB. The Incident Escalation Matrix governs incidents and
postmortems. The Security and Vulnerability Policy governs the
security checks in review and the patch schedule. The API and
Integration Standards govern API work specifically. The IP and
Confidentiality Policy governs the code itself, and the Data
Retention Policy governs how long development records are kept
(three years for operational records, seven years for security
records).

title: System Log Retention Policy
sourceName: Northwind Engineering System Log Retention Policy
body:
# System Log Retention Policy

## Purpose and Scope

This policy defines how long Northwind Systems retains system logs:
application logs, access logs, API logs, database logs, and security
logs from the products (Northwind Core, Atlas, Meridian) and from
internal systems. It is an engineering policy; the Data Retention
Policy covers business records (contracts, invoices, HR records,
customer data) and is owned by legal. Logs are not personal data in
the sense of the Privacy Policy and are not returned in data access
requests, but logs that contain personal data (for example, an email
address in a log line) are subject to the Privacy Policy's handling
rules while they exist. Questions go to the CTO's office.

## Retention Schedule

Logs are retained in three tiers. Raw logs (unaggregated application
and access logs) are kept for 90 days. Aggregated logs (metrics,
dashboards, rollups) are kept for 1 year. Security and audit logs
(authentication events, admin actions, permission changes, incident
logs) are kept for 7 years. The 7-year tier exists because the
security records feed investigations, audits, and the April and
October SOC 2 evidence. The tiers apply to production and staging
alike; development environments keep logs for 30 days. Logs are
deleted by the retention job at the end of their tier, and deletion
runs daily. Logs under a litigation hold (HLD-####) are exempt until
the hold is lifted, per the Data Retention Policy.

## What Counts as Security Logs

The 7-year tier covers: authentication events (successes and
failures), admin and permission changes, data export events, API key
creation and revocation, incident response records (INC-####), and
backup access records. Everything else falls in the 90-day raw tier
or the 1-year aggregated tier. When in doubt, engineering classifies
a log as security-related: the cost of keeping a log is small, and
the cost of missing an audit trail is not. Classification is set at
the logging source, reviewed annually, and documented in the log
registry. The CISO approves the classification list, and changes to
the list are logged.

## Access to Logs

Access to logs is role-based. Raw and aggregated logs: engineers,
support engineers for customer incidents, and the on-call rotation.
Security and audit logs: the CISO's team, the CTO, and engineering
managers; support engineers get read access to security logs only for
the customer they are working, and the access is logged. Log access
is granted per the access request process in the Security and
Vulnerability Policy, reviewed quarterly, and revoked on role change
or departure (see the Termination and Offboarding Policy's access
revocation). Logs are not copied to personal devices, and bulk exports
of security logs require the CISO's approval. Log access events
themselves are logged.

## Deletion and Backups

The retention job deletes raw logs older than 90 days and aggregated
logs older than 1 year daily, and the deletion is logged. Backups
containing logs expire on the backup schedule, which means log
deletion from backups can lag by up to 30 days; this lag is accepted
and documented. Security and audit logs are never excluded from
backups: the 7-year tier is backed up with the same schedule as the
rest of production data, per the Business Continuity Policy's RPO of
30 minutes. Log deletion is verified monthly by the engineering
manager, and the verification report is part of the SOC 2 evidence.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Data Retention Policy covers business records; this policy covers
logs, and where a record is both (for example, an invoice sent by
email, whose delivery log is a log), the longer period applies to the
record and the log tier applies to the log. The Privacy Policy
governs personal data found in logs while it exists. The Incident
Escalation Matrix sets the incident record requirements, which feed
the 7-year security tier. The Security and Vulnerability Policy
governs log access controls and the access request process. The
Customer Data Access Requests process does not return logs; DSAR
exports cover personal data, not log lines.

title: Board Reporting Calendar
body:
# Board Reporting Calendar

## Purpose and Confidentiality

This calendar defines the reporting rhythm between Northwind Systems
management and the board of directors. It is a private document: it
is visible only to the executive department, and board materials
are not distributed outside the executive team. The calendar is
owned by the CEO's office, and the General Counsel, Amelia Brooks,
administers the meeting logistics. The board of directors of
Northwind Systems meets quarterly, and the meetings are scheduled
for the second Tuesday of February, May, August, and November, in
Austin or by video. The December board meeting is added for budget
ratification, per the Budget Planning and Forecasting Policy.

## Meeting Schedule

The quarterly meetings fall on the second Tuesday of February, May,
August, and November. The December meeting (budget ratification)
is scheduled on the second Tuesday of December, and it is a
shorter session focused on the budget and the annual plan. Board
materials are due five business days before each meeting: the
packet includes the financials, the metrics, the pipeline, the
incident summary, and the action items from the prior meeting.
The packet is prepared by the CFO's office (financials), the CEO's
office (metrics and strategy), and legal (governance items).
Materials are distributed through the board portal, and printed
copies are provided only on request.

## Committee Schedule

The board has three standing committees. The audit committee meets
in April and October, aligned with the SOC 2 audit fieldwork per
the Regulatory Compliance Calendar, and reviews the audit evidence,
the financial controls, and the CISO's security metrics. The
compensation committee meets in June, ahead of the compensation
review, and reviews the executive compensation and the severance
policy (see the Executive Severance Policy). The governance
committee meets in January, and reviews board composition,
succession, and the annual director self-assessment. Committee
materials are due five business days before each committee
meeting, and committee minutes are included in the next board
packet.

## Board Compensation

Non-employee directors receive an annual retainer of $50,000, paid
quarterly, plus $2,500 per board meeting attended and $1,500 per
committee meeting attended. The chair of the audit committee
receives an additional $10,000 per year, and the chairs of the
compensation and governance committees receive an additional
$5,000 each. Directors do not receive equity grants beyond the
initial grant at appointment, which is set at the annual meeting.
Director compensation is reviewed by the governance committee in
January, and changes take effect at the annual meeting. Director
expenses follow the Travel Expense Policy and the Employee Expense
Policy, and are reimbursed within 10 business days of approval,
like employee expenses.

## Annual Meeting and Governance

The annual shareholder meeting is held in May, and proxy materials
are finalized 40 days before the meeting date. The annual report
draft goes to the board at the February meeting, covering the
December 31 year-end per the Regulatory Compliance Calendar's
annual filing deadlines. Board elections and director
appointments are effective at the annual meeting. The board
approves: the annual budget (December), the executive severance
policy (December), the M&A thresholds in the Merger and
Acquisition Approval Policy (as deals arise), and the appointment
and removal of officers. Officer appointments are proposed by the
CEO and approved by the board.

## Reporting to the Board

The CEO reports to the board at every meeting: revenue, pipeline,
headcount, product milestones, and the risk register. The CFO
reports the financials, the cash position, and the budget
variance. The CISO reports the security metrics at the May
meeting, per the Security and Vulnerability Policy, and at the
audit committee meetings. The CTO reports the engineering
metrics and the incident summary (SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents since
the prior meeting). ESC-4 complaints are reported at the next
meeting per the Customer Complaint Escalation Path, and disputes
above $100,000 are reported per the Dispute Resolution and
Arbitration Policy. The board packet template is maintained by
the CEO's office.

## Records and Confidentiality

Board materials, minutes, and committee records are retained for
ten years, which is longer than the standard retention in the
Data Retention Policy because board records are corporate
records; the General Counsel is the custodian. Board materials
are confidential under the IP and Confidentiality Policy and are
not shared outside the executive department. Directors sign the
director NDA under the NDA Policy at appointment. The board
calendar is reviewed annually in December, and changes to the
schedule are announced at least 30 days in advance except for
emergency meetings, which can be called by the CEO or the board
chair with 48 hours of notice.

title: Merger and Acquisition Approval Policy
sourceName: Northwind Executive Merger and Acquisition Approval Policy
body:
# Merger and Acquisition Approval Policy

## Purpose and Confidentiality

This policy governs how Northwind Systems evaluates and approves
mergers, acquisitions, and investments in other companies. It is a
private executive policy: it is visible only to the executive
department, and deal discussions are confidential under the IP and
Confidentiality Policy and the NDA Policy. The policy is owned by
the CEO, Dana Okafor, and the General Counsel, Amelia Brooks,
administers the deal process. This policy does not apply to
ordinary customer or vendor contracts, which follow the Contract
Review and Approval Policy. Every potential deal is registered in
the deal system with a code in the format M&A-#### before any
discussion with the counterparty.

## Approval Thresholds

Deals are approved by value. A deal with a total consideration below
$5 million is approved by the CEO alone, with the CFO informed.
A deal from $5 million to $25 million requires the approval of the
CEO, the CFO, and the General Counsel. A deal above $25 million
requires the board's approval, per the Board Reporting Calendar,
and the board must approve the deal before any binding commitment
is made. Total consideration includes cash, stock, assumed debt,
and earn-outs. The thresholds apply to the aggregate value of
related transactions: two deals with the same counterparty within
12 months are treated as one for approval purposes. Deals below
the thresholds but in a new market or a new product category are
reviewed by the board anyway, because of the strategic risk.

## Confidentiality and NDAs

No deal discussion starts without a signed NDA under the NDA
Policy, covering both sides. The NDA is signed before the first
meeting, and the deal code (M&A-####) is attached to the NDA. Deal
information is shared on a need-to-know basis: the deal team is
named by the CEO, and the team is limited to the executives, legal,
and the finance staff assigned to diligence. Deal information is
not discussed with employees outside the deal team, and the
standard rule is that the target company's name is not shared
inside Northwind until the deal is announced or the process ends.
A confidentiality breach during a deal is handled by the General
Counsel and is grounds for termination under the Termination and
Offboarding Policy.

## Due Diligence

Due diligence runs for at least 30 days for every deal, and the
diligence plan is approved by the General Counsel before it
starts. The diligence covers: financials (led by the CFO's team),
legal and contracts (led by legal), security and data (led by the
CISO's team, using the Security and Vulnerability Policy's
standards), HR and employment (led by the CHRO), and customer and
market (led by the COO). Diligence findings are consolidated in a
diligence report that the CEO reviews before any approval is
sought. A material finding (unreported liabilities, a security
breach, a customer concentration risk) is reported to the board
even for deals below the board threshold. Diligence materials are
retained for ten years.

## Exclusivity and Process Rules

Exclusivity agreements (the target agrees not to talk to other
buyers) are limited to 60 days, renewable once with the CEO's
approval. Letters of intent are approved at the level of the deal
threshold (the same approval chain as the final deal), because a
letter of intent commits Northwind to the process. No public
statement about a deal is made without the CEO's approval, and the
announcement plan is part of the board approval package for deals
above $25 million. Deals that involve the acquisition of a company
with employees trigger the HR integration plan, which the CHRO
prepares before signing, covering the Termination and Offboarding
Policy's application to the acquired staff.

## Integration and Post-Deal

After a deal closes, the integration plan is owned by the COO, with
the deal code (M&A-####) carried into the integration project. The
integration plan covers: systems and data migration (under the
Change Management Policy and the System Log Retention Policy),
customer communication (under the Customer Onboarding Checklist's
communication standards), and employee onboarding (under the
Recruiting and Interview Policy's handover). The acquired
company's contracts are reviewed under the Contract Review and
Approval Policy, and its vendors under the Vendor and Procurement
Policy. Integration milestones are reported to the board at the
next two board meetings, and the deal is reviewed for value
realization at the 12-month mark.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Contract Review and Approval Policy covers ordinary contracts;
deal documents (the purchase agreement, the exclusivity agreement)
are governed by this policy instead. The NDA Policy covers the
confidentiality agreements that start every deal. The Executive
Severance Policy's change of control provisions apply to
executives affected by a deal, and they are approved by the board
as part of the transaction. The Dispute Resolution and Arbitration
Policy governs post-deal disputes with the seller. The Board
Reporting Calendar covers the board approvals and the integration
reporting. The Data Retention Policy covers the retention of deal
records (ten years for board and deal records).

title: Executive Severance Policy
body:
# Executive Severance Policy

## Purpose and Confidentiality

This policy defines severance terms for Northwind Systems executive
officers: the CEO, the C-suite (CFO, CTO, CHRO, CISO, COO, General
Counsel), and vice presidents. It is a private board document: it is
visible only to the executive department, and its contents are not
shared with employees, managers, or the HR department except where
HR administers a departure under the Termination and Offboarding
Policy. The policy is approved by the board of directors and is
reviewed annually at the December board meeting (see the Board
Reporting Calendar). The standard employee termination terms are in
the Termination and Offboarding Policy; this policy covers only the
executive levels named here.

## CEO Severance

The CEO's severance is set by the board. If the CEO is terminated
without cause (or resigns for good reason, as defined in the CEO
employment agreement), the CEO receives: 24 months of base salary,
paid in normal payroll installments; 100% acceleration of unvested
equity, with all unvested options and restricted stock vesting on
the termination date; and continuation of health benefits for 24
months at the active employee rate. The CEO's severance requires
board approval and is not within the CEO's own authority. If the
CEO is terminated for cause, no severance is paid, and equity
unvested at termination is forfeited. The CEO's severance is not
subject to the non-solicit waiver process; the 12-month non-solicit
clause in the IP and Confidentiality Policy applies in all cases.

## C-Suite Severance

C-suite officers (CFO, CTO, CHRO, CISO, COO, General Counsel)
terminated without cause receive: 12 months of base salary, paid in
normal installments; 50% acceleration of unvested equity; and 12
months of health benefit continuation at the active employee rate.
C-suite severance is approved by the board, on the recommendation
of the CEO; the CEO cannot approve a C-suite severance alone. A
C-suite officer terminated for cause receives no severance. A
C-suite officer who resigns voluntarily receives no severance,
except in a good-reason resignation as defined in their employment
agreement (material reduction in role, relocation without consent,
or a breach of the agreement by the company). Good-reason
resignations are reviewed by the board.

## VP Severance

Vice presidents terminated without cause receive: 6 months of base
salary, paid in normal installments; no equity acceleration
(unvested equity is forfeited, and vested equity is exercisable for
90 days per the Termination and Offboarding Policy); and 6 months
of health benefit continuation. VP severance is approved by the CEO
with the CHRO's review; the board is not involved except for the
annual review of the policy. A VP terminated for cause receives no
severance. VP severance does not include bonus or commission
payouts beyond what is earned under the Sales Commission Plan, and
the commission plan's clawback rules apply to any commission paid
in the 90 days before termination.

## Change of Control

In a change of control (a merger or acquisition covered by the
Merger and Acquisition Approval Policy), the severance terms above
are replaced by the change of control provisions: executives who
are terminated without cause within 12 months of the change of
control receive their severance under this policy, doubled: the CEO
receives 24 months (unchanged, as the base already reflects the
change of control), and C-suite officers receive 24 months with
100% equity acceleration. The change of control provisions apply
only if the executive's role is eliminated or materially reduced;
an executive who stays in an equivalent role is not eligible. The
board approves the change of control provisions as part of the
transaction approval under the Merger and Acquisition Approval
Policy.

## Board Approval and Administration

All executive severance agreements require board approval, including
the CEO's own agreement (approved by the board without the CEO's
vote). The board reviews the severance policy annually at the
December board meeting, and any change to the policy takes effect
on January 1 of the following year. HR administers the payments
under the Termination and Offboarding Policy's final pay rules (72
hours for earned pay), but HR does not set the terms and does not
negotiate them. Severance agreements are contracts under the
Contract Review and Approval Policy's records rules: they are
retained for seven years after the agreement ends, per the Data
Retention Policy. The board's compensation committee reviews the
severance terms at its June meeting (see the Board Reporting
Calendar).

## Confidentiality of This Policy

This policy is private. Its existence and its terms are not
published on the intranet, are not in the Employee Handbook, and
are not described in any employee-facing document. The standard
termination documents (the Termination and Offboarding Policy)
refer to executive terms only as "terms per the executive
agreement." Directors and executives who share this policy outside
the executive department breach the IP and Confidentiality Policy,
and the breach is handled by the board. Questions about this
policy go to the General Counsel, Amelia Brooks, who is the
custodian of the executive agreements.

title: Budget Planning and Forecasting
sourceName: Northwind Finance Budget Planning and Forecasting
body:
# Budget Planning and Forecasting

## Purpose and Ownership

This document describes how Northwind Systems plans and forecasts its
budget. It is owned by finance, and its readers are the finance team and
the executive leadership. The budget cycle runs from the calendar year
fiscal year (January 1 to December 31). The CFO, Marcus Webb, owns the
process, and the CEO, Dana Okafor, approves the final budget at the
December board meeting, which is covered by the Board Reporting Calendar.
Department heads are responsible for submitting their department budgets
on time; the process is the same every year, and the deadlines in this
document are fixed.

## Budget Cycle Timeline

The annual cycle has five milestones. June 1: finance publishes the
budget instructions and templates. July 15: department heads submit
their initial budget requests. August 15: finance returns first-pass
feedback and departments revise. September 30: departments submit final
budgets. November 1: the executive team reviews the consolidated budget
with the CFO, and the CEO approves it. December board meeting (the
second Tuesday of December): the board ratifies the budget. The
November 1 review is the last point at which department totals can
change; after that, changes require the CFO's written approval. The
merit increase pool for the following year is fixed during the
September 30 submission at 3% of payroll by default.

## Department Budget Structure

Each department budget has four envelopes: payroll, travel and
expenses, tools and software, and capital. Payroll includes salaries,
bonus accruals, and contractor spend, and is validated against the
Salary Bands document by HR before submission. Travel and expenses are
planned at 80% of the prior year's actual spend by default, and any
department requesting more must attach a written justification. Tools
and software budgets are reviewed by finance for overlap with the
corporate tool list maintained by IT. Capital (equipment, office
furnishings) is approved separately by operations under the Vendor and
Procurement Policy's thresholds, but the budget line is set here.

## Forecasting During the Year

Forecasting is a quarterly activity. Finance publishes a rolling
forecast on the 15th of February, May, August, and November, comparing
actuals to the budget and projecting the year-end position. Department
heads review the forecast with finance within five business days of
publication. A department forecast that exceeds its budget by more than
5% triggers a formal review with the CFO. Revenue forecasting is owned
by finance with input from sales: the sales forecast feeds the
commission accrual (see the Sales Commission Plan) and the cash
projection. The forecast is not a commitment; only the approved budget
controls spending, and the Vendor and Procurement Policy's approval
thresholds apply to actual purchases.

## Spending Rules

Department budgets are annual and do not roll over; unused budget at
December 31 is returned to the company, except for the training budget
rules in the Training and Development Budget. Mid-year reallocation
between envelopes within a department is allowed up to $50,000 per
reallocation with the CFO's approval, and reallocation between
departments is not allowed at all. Hiring beyond the budgeted headcount
requires the CEO's approval and is reviewed against the approved
headcount plan; the Recruiting and Interview Policy's offer thresholds
still apply. Emergency spending above the department budget requires
the CFO's approval and is reported to the board at the next board
meeting.

## Budget vs Actuals Reporting

Finance publishes a monthly budget-vs-actuals report to department heads
by the 10th of the following month. The report shows actuals, budget,
variance, and a variance explanation column that departments must
complete for variances above 10%. The April and October SOC 2 audits
include a sample of the monthly reports, and the annual audit of
financial statements happens in January, using the December 31
year-end. The board receives a summary of the year-end position at the
February board meeting, per the Board Reporting Calendar. Variance
reports are retained for seven years under the Data Retention Policy.

## Key Planning Assumptions

The standard planning assumptions are published with the June 1
instructions and rarely change: revenue growth of 15% year over year,
merit pool of 3% of payroll, travel budget at 80% of prior year actuals,
and a 2% of payroll training allocation. Headcount planning assumes one
new hire for every $350,000 of incremental annual recurring revenue
booked, which ties hiring to the sales forecast. Exchange rates for the
budget use the November finance rate and are fixed for the budget year.
The CFO can revise planning assumptions mid-year only for material
events, and any revision is communicated to department heads within five
business days.

title: Contractor Expense Policy
body:
# Contractor Expense Policy

## Scope

This policy covers expenses incurred by contractors, consultants, and
temporary staff working with Northwind Systems. Contractors are not
employees, and their expense rules differ from the Employee Expense
Policy in three important ways: reimbursement takes 30 business days,
approval is by finance only (no manager approval chain), and the receipt
threshold is $50 instead of $25. This policy is administered by finance
and is shared with operations because operations manages contractor
agreements and vendor onboarding. Questions go to expenses@northwind.example
with the contractor's invoice code.

## Reimbursable Expenses

Reimbursable contractor expenses are limited to those written into the
contractor's agreement or statement of work: travel to Northwind sites
or customer sites, project-specific software licenses, and materials
directly consumed by the engagement. Expenses not in the agreement are
not reimbursable, even if an employee sponsor approves them informally.
Contractors do not receive per-diem meal rates: meals are reimbursed at
actual cost with receipts, capped at $60 per day, and only when the
contractor is traveling away from their home base. Client entertainment
by contractors is not reimbursable unless the agreement explicitly
includes it. The employee sponsor (the person managing the contractor)
can answer questions about what the agreement covers.

## Receipts and Documentation

Receipts are required for every expense of $50 or more. Expenses under
$50 do not need a receipt but must be itemized. There is no signed
statement route for missing receipts; a missing receipt over $50 makes
that line non-reimbursable. Each claim line needs the date, purpose,
and the agreement code (CT-####) from the contractor's contract. Claims
are submitted through the contractor portal, not the employee expense
system. Falsified claims are a breach of the contractor agreement and
lead to termination of the engagement and removal from the vendor list
under the Vendor and Procurement Policy.

## Submission and Payment Timing

Contractors submit expense claims within 30 days of the expense date.
Claims are paid within 30 business days of approval, not 10 business
days like employee expenses, because contractor payments run through the
vendor payment cycle with a single monthly run. The finance team approves
or rejects claims within five business days of submission. Rejected
claims come back with the reason and can be resubmitted once, corrected,
within 10 business days. Payment is made by bank transfer to the
contractor's registered account, and the Contractor Expense Policy does
not offer payroll-run reimbursement or corporate cards. Late claims (over
30 days) are paid in the following month's run without penalty but are
flagged on the contractor's account.

## Approval and Controls

All contractor expense approvals are made by finance staff; the employee
sponsor's role is to confirm the expense relates to the engagement, and
finance makes the payment decision. The finance manager approves claims
up to $2,500, and the finance director approves claims above $2,500;
there is no VP or CFO step because the claim total is capped by the
agreement's expense limit, which is set at contract signing and
registered in the vendor system. Contractor claims above $5,000 in a
single month are reviewed by the CFO as part of the vendor payment run.
Contractors cannot hold corporate cards under any circumstances, and
the Corporate Card Policy does not apply to them.

## Expenses for Contractors at Northwind Sites

Contractors working at Northwind offices follow the Office and Facilities
Policy for access and safety, but their expense claims still follow this
policy. Meals at the office cafeteria or canteen are not reimbursable.
If a contractor needs equipment (laptop, badge, access card), it is
provisioned by operations through the vendor system and returned when
the engagement ends, following the same 30-day return rule as the
Equipment Return Policy; lost or damaged equipment is charged against
the contractor's final invoice. Contractors are not eligible for the
training budget, the referral program, or any employee benefit in the
Employee Handbook.

## Relationship to Other Policies

Contractor invoices for services are paid under the Invoicing and
Payment Terms Policy's Net 30 terms and the Vendor and Procurement
Policy's approval thresholds. Contractors who also receive employee
referral bonuses or commissions must not: those payments are for
employees only. If a contractor is later hired as an employee, their
expense rules change on their first day of employment, and any claims
pending at that point are paid under the contractor rules to keep the
audit trail clean. Disputes about contractor expenses follow the
Dispute Resolution and Arbitration Policy like any other contract
dispute.

title: Corporate Card Policy
body:
# Corporate Card Policy

## Issuance and Eligibility

Corporate cards at Northwind Systems are issued to employees whose role
requires regular business purchasing: managers, directors, and finance
staff. Cards are issued by finance and are the property of the company.
Requests for a card are submitted by the manager to finance with a
business justification; the finance manager approves or denies within
five business days. Cards are issued with the cardholder's name and a
card code in the format CC-####. Contractors can never hold corporate
cards, per the Contractor Expense Policy. A cardholder who changes role
or leaves the company returns the card on their last day, under the
Termination and Offboarding Policy's equipment rules.

## Spending Limits

Monthly spending limits are set by role: $10,000 per month for standard
cardholders (managers), $25,000 per month for directors, and $50,000
per month for VPs and above. Finance staff receive the limit matching
their role. The limit resets on the first of each month and applies to
the calendar month, not a rolling 30 days. A single purchase above
$5,000 requires pre-approval by the finance manager, even if the monthly
limit would cover it. Temporary limit increases (up to 60 days) are
approved by the finance director. The card system blocks purchases that
would exceed the monthly limit; there is no overdraft.

## Permitted and Prohibited Purchases

Cards are for business purchases only: software subscriptions, client
meals, travel booked outside the portal in approved cases, office
supplies, and conference fees. Personal purchases are strictly
prohibited at any amount, including personal meals, personal fuel, and
personal travel. Gift cards are prohibited in any amount and are
grounds for immediate card revocation and disciplinary review. Cash
advances are not available on corporate cards. Split purchases (splitting
one purchase into multiple transactions to stay under a limit or
approval threshold) are prohibited. Alcohol purchases are permitted for
client entertainment up to $100 per event; anything beyond that needs
manager pre-approval.

## Expense Reporting for Card Purchases

Card purchases are imported into the expense system automatically, and
the cardholder must allocate and document each transaction within 30
days of the purchase date, with receipts at $25 and above, exactly like
the Employee Expense Policy. Undocumented transactions are flagged at
day 30 and the card is blocked at day 45 until the report is completed.
Card expenses do not require reimbursement (finance pays the card
directly) but they require approval under the same thresholds: manager
approval up to $2,500, VP from $2,500 to $10,000, CFO above $10,000.
Personal charges found on a card are recovered from the cardholder's
pay under the payroll deduction process and reported to the CHRO.

## Card Security and Loss

Cardholders are responsible for the security of their card and its
details. Report a lost or stolen card immediately to finance and block
it in the card portal; the card is blocked within minutes, and a
replacement arrives in 5 to 7 business days. The cardholder is not
liable for fraudulent charges made after the loss is reported. Card
details are never stored in personal password managers; they live in
the corporate vault. Suspected fraud on a statement is disputed through
the card portal within 10 business days of the statement date, and
finance tracks disputes to resolution. Sharing card details with anyone,
including colleagues, is prohibited; each cardholder has their own card.

## Card Reviews and Audits

Finance reviews card statements monthly and audits a sample of
cardholders each quarter for compliance with this policy. The audit
checks: documentation completeness, business purpose, limit adherence,
and prohibited purchase categories. Findings are sent to the cardholder
and their manager. Repeated violations (two in a rolling 12-month
period) lead to card revocation for 90 days; a third violation leads to
permanent revocation and a note in the employee's HR record. The
quarterly audit results are summarized for the CFO and included in the
April and October SOC 2 audit evidence, per the Regulatory Compliance
Calendar.

## Cards for Offsite and Travel

Cards are the preferred payment method for business travel: the Travel
Expense Policy's rules apply to travel purchases on cards, including the
per-diem (which is paid as reimbursement, never as a card cash advance),
hotel caps, and airfare class rules. Travel booked through the corporate
travel portal is paid by finance directly; cards are for incidental
travel costs. International purchases are converted at the card
processor's rate, and the difference from the monthly finance rate is
not reimbursable. Card rewards accrue to the company, never to the
cardholder, and using a personal card to earn rewards on business
purchases is permitted but the expenses still follow the Employee
Expense Policy.

title: Employee Expense Policy
body:
# Employee Expense Policy

## Scope

This policy covers business expenses incurred by Northwind Systems
employees and reimbursed by the company. It is the general expense
policy: the Travel Expense Policy overrides it for travel-specific items
(airfare, hotels, per-diem), and the Corporate Card Policy covers
purchases on company cards. Contractors are not covered here; their
rules are in the Contractor Expense Policy. Expense claims are submitted
through the expense system, which assigns each report a code in the
format EXP-####. The policy is owned by finance, and questions go to
expenses@northwind.example.

## What Is Reimbursable

Reimbursable expenses are ordinary and necessary business costs: office
supplies bought out of pocket, client meals, software subscriptions used
for work, books, parking, and work-related mileage. Personal expenses are
never reimbursable, including personal meals, commuting between home and
the office, and personal upgrades. Client meals are reimbursable up to
$150 per person including tax, with the client's name and business
purpose on the receipt. Subscriptions used for both work and personal
use are reimbursable only if the work use is the primary purpose, and
the finance team may ask for a justification. Gift cards are not
reimbursable in any amount; buying gift cards on a corporate card is a
violation of the Corporate Card Policy.

## Receipts and Documentation

Receipts are required for every expense of $25 or more. Under $25,
receipts are not required but the expense must still be itemized in the
report. A missing receipt for an expense over $25 can be replaced with a
signed statement from the employee explaining the purchase, but the
statement route is limited to three expenses per calendar year. Every
report line needs the business purpose, the date, and the attendees for
meals. The expense system flags reports missing required fields, and
finance returns incomplete reports within three business days instead of
approving them. Falsifying an expense is gross misconduct and is handled
under the Termination and Offboarding Policy.

## Submission Deadlines

Expense reports must be submitted within 30 days of the expense date, or
within 30 days of the trip's end for travel. Reports submitted after the
deadline are still reviewed but are flagged, and two late submissions in
a rolling 12-month period trigger a written reminder from finance. The
deadline exists so expenses land in the right accounting period; the
fiscal year closes on December 31, and expenses from the prior year must
be submitted by January 31 to be paid. Reimbursement is paid within 10
business days of approval, in the next payroll run. Approval happens
within five business days of submission, so the full cycle from
submission to payment is at most 15 business days when the report is
clean.

## Approval Thresholds

Approval authority is based on the total of the report: managers approve
reports up to $2,500, department VPs approve reports from $2,500 to
$10,000, and the CFO approves reports above $10,000. Approvers cannot
approve their own reports; a manager's own report goes to their manager,
and the CFO's reports are approved by the CEO. Reports above $10,000
need a business case attached. The thresholds apply to the report total,
not to individual lines, so a report with ten $300 lines still needs VP
approval. Approval is not rubber-stamping: approvers review the business
purpose, and finance audits a sample of 10% of approved reports each
quarter.

## Mileage and Out-of-Pocket

Mileage for personal vehicles used on business is reimbursed at $0.65 per
mile, the same rate used by the Travel Expense Policy. Mileage is
calculated by the expense system from the addresses entered; manually
entered distances above 50 miles need manager approval. Out-of-pocket
purchases for the company (for example, paying a vendor COD) are
reimbursed under the same rules, and any single out-of-pocket purchase
above $500 should have been approved in advance by the manager. Currency:
expenses in foreign currency are converted at the monthly finance rate,
and the system shows the rate used on the report.

## Relationship to Other Policies

Expenses for travel use the rates in the Travel Expense Policy: per-diem
meals of $65/$85/$75, hotel caps of $250/$350/$300, and the airfare
rules. Training expenses follow the Training and Development Budget
($2,500 annual allocation, manager approval). Reimbursement for departing
employees is included in the final pay process of the Termination and
Offboarding Policy, subject to the same deadlines. Corporate card
holders follow the Corporate Card Policy, which requires the same
receipts and deadlines; card expenses do not need a separate
reimbursement because they are paid directly by finance.

title: Invoicing and Payment Terms
sourceName: Northwind Finance Invoicing and Payment Terms
body:
# Invoicing and Payment Terms

## Standard Payment Terms

Northwind Systems invoices customers under standard Net 30 terms: payment
is due 30 calendar days from the invoice date. Annual plans are invoiced
upfront for the full year on the contract start date, and monthly plans
are invoiced on the first of each month. Invoices are issued through the
billing system with codes in the format INV-####, and are sent by email
from billing@northwind.example on the invoice date. The payment terms
are written into every contract (see the Contract Review and Approval
Policy) and cannot be changed by sales at the point of sale; a Net 60
exception exists for enterprise contracts above $250,000 in annual
value, approved by the CFO and noted in the contract.

## Currency and FX

The default invoice currency is USD. UK customers are invoiced in GBP
and Singapore customers in SGD, based on the customer's billing address;
other customers are invoiced in USD. Currency conversion uses the
monthly finance rate, published on the first business day of each month
and applied to all invoices issued that month. The rate is fixed for the
invoice; FX differences on payment are the customer's risk unless the
contract says otherwise. Customers can request USD invoicing regardless
of location, and the request is granted by the billing team without
approval. The Tax Withholding Policy covers how taxes appear on
invoices.

## Late Payment

Payment is late after the due date plus a 15-day grace period. From day
16 past due, a late fee of 1.5% per month applies on the outstanding
balance, calculated daily and added to the next invoice. The billing
system sends reminders at day 0 (due date), day 15 (grace ending), and
day 30 past due. Service suspension happens at 45 days past due: the
customer receives a 7-day written notice before suspension, and
suspension stops access to all Northwind products but does not cancel
the contract. Accounts are unsuspended within 24 hours of payment in
full or an agreed payment plan. Payment plans are approved by the
finance manager and can extend payment by up to 90 days.

## Payment Methods

Customers can pay by card (all major cards, processed through the
billing portal), bank transfer, or direct debit. Card payments on annual
plans incur no surcharge; card payments on monthly plans incur a 2%
processing fee unless the customer is on a prepaid annual plan. Bank
transfers are free and take 2 to 5 business days to clear; the invoice
is marked paid on clearance, not on instruction. Direct debit is
available in the US, UK, and Singapore and is the recommended method for
monthly plans. Refunds to any of these methods follow the Refund Policy:
processing within 5 to 10 business days, returned to the original
payment method.

## Invoicing for Partners and Resellers

Partner-sourced business is invoiced to the partner, not the end
customer, when the partner is the reseller of record; the Partner
Program Policy defines when a partner is the reseller of record. Partner
invoices follow the same Net 30 terms. Partner commissions are not
invoiced: they are paid separately under the Partner Program Policy on a
quarterly cycle. Discounts applied to invoices must match an approved
discount under the Discount Approval Policy; an invoice with an
unapproved discount is rejected by the billing system and returned to
sales. Quotes that led to the order are referenced on the invoice
(QT-####), which lets billing verify the price against the Proposal and
Quote Process.

## Billing Disputes

Invoice disputes are logged through support with a ticket, and the
billing team responds within five business days. A disputed amount is
not late while the dispute is open, but the undisputed portion remains
due under the original terms. Disputes that are not resolved within 30
days move to the Customer Complaint Escalation Path (ESC-3) and, for
amounts above $10,000, to the Dispute Resolution and Arbitration Policy.
Credit notes are issued only by finance, with a code CN-####, and must
reference the original invoice. Billing errors found by the customer
are corrected under the Refund Policy's billing error exception, in
full, with no window.

## Record Keeping

Invoice records are kept for seven years after the invoice date, per
the Data Retention Policy, and the seven-year retention also applies to
credit notes and payment records. The billing system is the system of
record; emailed invoices are for convenience. The Regulatory Compliance
Calendar lists the audit checkpoints for billing records (April and
October SOC 2 audits). Finance reconciles invoices to revenue monthly,
and any invoice older than 90 days that is neither paid nor disputed is
escalated to the CFO in the weekly billing review.

title: Procurement Forms and Workflow Guide
