title: Scheduled Maintenance Policy
body:
# Scheduled Maintenance Policy

## Purpose

This policy governs scheduled maintenance that requires downtime or
that risks customer impact at Northwind Systems: infrastructure
maintenance, database maintenance, and environment work that cannot
run inside the normal change windows. It is owned by operations and
is shared with engineering, which performs the work. The Change
Management Policy covers code changes and configuration changes,
which run in the Tuesday and Thursday 10:00-14:00 CT windows; this
policy covers the separate maintenance window and its notice rules.
Maintenance is logged with change codes (CHG-####) and maintenance
codes (MT-####).

## Maintenance Window

The standard maintenance window is Saturday, 02:00 to 04:00 UTC
(which is Friday 21:00 to 23:00 CT and Saturday 10:00 to 12:00
Singapore time). All downtime maintenance runs in this window.
Maintenance outside the window requires the COO's approval, and
out-of-window maintenance is limited to: emergency maintenance
(see below) and maintenance that cannot wait, approved case by
case. The window exists because it is the lowest-traffic period
across the three regions; the Saturday window is not changed for
regional holidays, but maintenance that falls on a major holiday
in two of the three regions is moved to the next Saturday.

## Notice Requirements

Customers receive 72 hours of notice for scheduled maintenance,
through the status page and email, with the start time, the
expected duration, and the impact. The customer notification is
sent 24 hours before the window starts, once the maintenance is
confirmed. Maintenance that affects a specific customer's data
(an account-level operation) is additionally announced to that
customer by their CSM 5 business days in advance. The notice
includes the maintenance code (MT-####). Maintenance is
cancelled or rescheduled with 24 hours of notice if the
pre-checks fail; a reschedule moves to the next Saturday window
unless the COO approves an earlier slot.

## Emergency Maintenance

Emergency maintenance is maintenance required to protect service
(imminent failure, security patch that cannot wait for a
Saturday window, or recovery from an incident). Emergency
maintenance requires the COO's approval, or the CTO's approval if
the COO is unavailable, and it is logged with a CHG-#### code
and the emergency designation. The customer impact is announced
as soon as the maintenance is approved: the status page is
updated within 1 hour, and affected customers are emailed with
the impact and the expected duration. Emergency maintenance that
runs longer than 2 hours is reviewed by the COO, and a
post-maintenance review is attached within 5 business days.
Three emergency maintenances in a quarter trigger a review of
the infrastructure backlog by the COO and the CTO.

## Maintenance Types

Maintenance falls into three types. Infrastructure: hardware,
network, and cloud service maintenance, with no data impact.
Database: index rebuilds, archive moves, and version upgrades,
with possible brief read-only periods. Environment: staging and
non-production work that does not need a window (staging work
runs any time), and production-adjacent work (monitoring,
logging) that runs in the window. Database maintenance is
scheduled first-come in the window, and the operations team
queues the month's maintenance on the last Friday of the prior
month. Maintenance that can run without downtime (rolling
updates) runs in the Tuesday and Thursday change windows under
the Change Management Policy instead of the maintenance window.

## Maintenance Records

Maintenance records (the MT-#### code, the window, the notice
sent, the outcome, and the post-review) are kept in the change
system and retained for three years under the System Log
Retention Policy's operational records. The monthly maintenance
report (count, duration, incidents caused) goes to the COO, and
maintenance that causes an incident is reviewed under the
Incident Escalation Matrix. The April and October SOC 2 audits
include the maintenance records and the notice evidence. The
maintenance calendar is published quarterly, and the status page
shows the upcoming maintenance 72 hours in advance per the
notice rules.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Change Management Policy covers code and configuration
changes in the Tuesday and Thursday windows; this policy covers
downtime maintenance in the Saturday window, and the two
policies cross-reference each other's windows. The Channel and
Hours Policy governs how maintenance notices reach customers
through the status page. The Incident Escalation Matrix governs
maintenance that causes incidents. The Business Continuity
Policy covers maintenance during a disaster declaration (the
COO can suspend all maintenance). The On-Call Rotation covers
who is on call during the maintenance window.

title: Vendor and Procurement Policy
sourceName: Northwind Operations Vendor and Procurement Policy
body:
# Vendor and Procurement Policy

## Purpose

This policy governs how Northwind Systems buys from vendors: vendor
onboarding, purchase approvals, and vendor management. It is owned
by operations and shared with finance, which pays the invoices.
The policy applies to goods and services for internal use
(software, equipment, office supplies, contractors, professional
services). It does not apply to customer contracts (see the
Contract Review and Approval Policy) or to the Partner Program.
Every purchase is a purchase order with a code in the format
PO-####, and purchases without a PO are not paid.

## Purchase Approval Thresholds

Purchase orders are approved by value. Purchase orders below $5,000
are approved by the requesting manager. Purchase orders from
$5,000 to $50,000 are approved by the operations director.
Purchase orders above $50,000 require the CFO's approval. The
thresholds apply to the PO total, and splitting a purchase into
multiple POs to stay under a threshold is prohibited and is
reviewed in the quarterly audit. Recurring purchases (monthly
subscriptions) are approved once per year at the annual value and
then flow monthly without re-approval. The approval chain is
separate from the budget check: the PO system checks the
department budget (Budget Planning and Forecasting Policy) before
the approval chain runs, and a PO without budget is blocked.

## Vendor Onboarding

New vendors are onboarded before the first PO: the vendor completes
the vendor application with tax registration details (per the Tax
Withholding Policy), banking information, and a signed vendor NDA
(per the NDA Policy). Vendors processing personal data sign the
data processing terms under the Privacy Policy, and their data
handling is assessed by the CISO's team. Onboarding takes up to 10
business days, and vendors are registered with codes in the format
VD-####. Contractors are onboarded as vendors with their agreement
(CT-####) attached, per the Contractor Expense Policy. Vendors
with a compliance failure (a security finding or a failed
reference check) are not onboarded, and the decision is logged.

## Quotes and Competition

Competitive quotes are required: two quotes for purchases of
$10,000 or more, and three quotes for purchases of $50,000 or
more. The quotes are attached to the PO, and the operations
director reviews the comparison for the $50,000 tier. Single
source purchases (one vendor can supply) need a written
justification from the requester and are approved at one level
above the PO threshold. The quote requirement does not apply to:
renewals of existing vendors within 10% of the prior price,
regulated utilities, and emergency purchases under the emergency
rules of this policy. Quote documents are retained with the PO
records.

## Contractors

Contractors are engaged through this policy and the Contractor
Expense Policy: the engagement is a PO with a statement of work,
the contractor's agreement is registered (CT-####), and the
contractor's expenses follow the Contractor Expense Policy.
Contractor rates are set at engagement and reviewed annually; a
rate increase above 5% requires the operations director's
approval. Contractor engagements follow the NDA Policy (vendor
NDA) and the IP and Confidentiality Policy's assignment clause,
which must be signed before work starts. Contractors are
onboarded and offboarded by operations with IT, and their access
is revoked within 24 hours of the engagement end (see the
Security and Vulnerability Policy).

## Vendor Management

Vendors are reviewed annually: security posture (via the CISO's
team), performance, and price. The annual review produces a
vendor scorecard, and vendors below the threshold are put on a
30-day improvement plan or replaced. Critical vendors (those whose
failure would break customer service) are identified with the
Business Continuity Policy's vendor dependency list, and their
failover plans are tested in the quarterly DR test. Vendor
invoices are paid under Net 30 terms per the Invoicing and
Payment Terms Policy, and the PO is matched to the invoice before
payment: an invoice without a matching PO is returned. Late vendor
payments are reported to the CFO, and vendor disputes follow the
Dispute Resolution and Arbitration Policy.

## Records and Audits

PO and vendor records are retained for seven years under the Data
Retention Policy's financial records rule. The quarterly
procurement audit reviews: PO approvals against thresholds,
splitting, quote compliance, and vendor onboarding completion.
The audit findings feed the SOC 2 audit evidence (April and
October). The procurement report (spend by category, vendor
concentration, quote compliance) goes to the COO and the CFO
quarterly, and vendor concentration above 30% of spend in a
single vendor is flagged to the CFO for a diversification
review.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Contractor Expense Policy governs contractor expenses and
payment. The Vendor NDA comes from the NDA Policy, and vendor
contracts follow the Contract Review and Approval Policy's
thresholds (a vendor agreement above $100,000 needs legal
review). The Budget Planning and Forecasting Policy funds the
POs. The Tax Withholding Policy governs the tax forms vendors
complete. The Business Continuity Policy covers critical vendor
failover. The Dispute Resolution and Arbitration Policy governs
vendor disputes. The Office and Facilities Policy covers
facilities purchases within this policy's thresholds.

title: Sales Commission Plan
body:
# Sales Commission Plan

## Purpose and Confidentiality

This document defines the commission plan for the Northwind Systems
sales team. It contains the commission rates and is confidential: it
is visible only to sales managers and directors, and the rates are
not shared with individual reps (reps see their own plan summary in
the commission portal, which states their rate without the full
table). The plan is owned by the VP of Sales with finance oversight,
and the CFO approves the plan each year in December for the following
year. The plan year is the calendar year, and the plan applies to
sales roles: account executives, account managers, and sales
directors. Questions go to the commission administrator in finance.

## Commission Rates

Commission is paid as a percentage of invoiced ACV. New business
(deals with customers who have never subscribed, or who were
churned for more than 12 months) pays 8% of ACV. Renewals and
expansion (additional seats or modules on an existing account) pay
4% of ACV. The rate applies to the invoiced amount: a deal signed
with a discount pays commission on the discounted ACV, per the
Discount Approval Policy. There is no commission cap, and there is
no accelerator. Professional services revenue does not earn
commission. Partner-sourced deals are not commissioned to the rep;
they are paid under the Partner Program Policy, and the rep's role
in a partner deal is limited to the registration credit rules of
that policy.

## Commission Calculation

Commission is calculated on invoices paid, not on contracts signed:
the commission for a deal is earned when the customer's first
invoice is paid in full (for annual plans) or when the second
monthly invoice is paid (for monthly plans). The commission base is
the ACV on the invoice, converted at the monthly finance rate for
non-USD invoices (see the Invoicing and Payment Terms Policy).
Commission is calculated by the commission administrator in finance
by the 10th of the month for the prior month's paid invoices.
Disputed or partially paid invoices do not earn commission until
the dispute is resolved under the Invoicing and Payment Terms
Policy.

## Payment Schedule

Commission is paid monthly, with the last paycheck of the month
(the final Friday), covering invoices paid in the prior month.
The payment schedule is monthly, not quarterly, and there is no
holding period beyond the invoice payment requirement. Commission
statements are available in the commission portal by the 15th of
the month, and discrepancies are resolved with the commission
administrator within 10 business days of the statement. Commission
is paid on the normal payroll and is taxed as ordinary income.
Departing salespeople receive earned commission (invoices paid
before their last day) in their final pay under the Termination
and Offboarding Policy; unearned pipeline does not vest.

## Clawbacks

Commission is clawed back when the underlying invoice is refunded or
the account cancels and is refunded, under the Refund Policy's
windows (14 calendar days for annual plans, 7 days for monthly
plans) or the refund exceptions. The clawback window is 90 days
from the commission payment: a refund inside the window claws back
the commission in full from the next commission payment, and a
refund outside the window is absorbed by the company, not the rep.
A rep who leaves with a clawback outstanding has the amount
deducted from final pay under the Termination and Offboarding
Policy. Clawbacks are tracked by the commission administrator, and
the clawback rate is reported quarterly to the CFO.

## Plan Administration

The plan is administered by the commission administrator in finance,
with the sales VP reviewing the monthly calculations. Rate changes
are made only at year-end, by the CFO's approval, and are announced
with the December plan letter; mid-year changes require the CEO's
approval and apply only to new deals. The plan letter is issued to
sales managers each January. Commission disputes follow the
Dispute Resolution and Arbitration Policy's negotiation step, with
the commission administrator's decision appealable to the CFO.
Commission records are retained for seven years under the Data
Retention Policy, and the plan is included in the April and October
SOC 2 audit evidence as a financial control.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Discount Approval Policy determines the discount, which sets
the commission base. The Refund Policy and the Invoicing and
Payment Terms Policy determine when commission is earned and when
it is clawed back. The Partner Program Policy governs partner
deals, which are not commissioned. The Referral Program pays
employee referral bonuses ($2,000 per customer) which are separate
from commission and are not paid to sales roles for their own
deals. The Termination and Offboarding Policy governs final pay
and clawback deductions. The Territory and Account Assignment
Policy determines which rep owns an account for commission
purposes: commission follows the account owner on the closing
date, and account transfers are handled by that policy.

title: Discount Approval Policy
body:
# Discount Approval Policy

## Purpose

This policy defines who can approve discounts on Northwind product
pricing, and how much. It is owned by sales and is shared with
finance, which enforces the discounts at billing time. The policy
applies to discounts on annual contract value (ACV) for Northwind
Core, Atlas, and Meridian, and to discounts on professional services.
It does not apply to partner pricing, which is set under the Partner
Program Policy, and it does not apply to referral payouts, which are
fixed amounts under the Referral Program. Discounts are set on the
order form at quote time, per the Proposal and Quote Process, and an
unapproved discount is rejected by the billing system.

## Discount Tiers and Approval Authority

Discounts are measured as a percentage off list price, on ACV.
Approval authority: discounts below 10% are approved by the sales
manager (the rep's manager). Discounts from 10% to 20% are approved
by the sales VP. Discounts above 20% require the CFO's approval, and
the CFO reviews them in the weekly pricing review. A discount above
30% is not available at any approval level: the deal is repriced,
restructured, or declined. The tiers apply to the total discount on
the deal, not per line item: stacking a 10% product discount with a
5% services discount is a 15% deal, needing VP approval. Discounts
are expressed as whole numbers, and the pricing system rounds at
quote time.

## Rules of Application

Discounts apply to ACV, which is the annualized value of the
contract, including all seats and modules. Discounts do not apply to:
taxes, one-time setup fees (which have their own fixed pricing),
partner-sourced deals (which follow partner pricing), or add-on
purchases made after the initial contract (which are quoted at list
price unless a new discount approval is attached). A discount
approved for a renewal must be re-approved: the renewal is a new
quote under the Proposal and Quote Process, and prior approvals do
not carry over. Discounts cannot be combined with the partner
program pricing: a deal is either a direct deal with a discount or a
partner deal with partner pricing, never both.

## Discount Justification

Every discount above 10% requires a justification in the pricing
system: the competitive situation, the deal size, or the strategic
reason. Discounts above 20% require a written one-page note from the
sales VP explaining the deal, attached to the quote. The CFO can
reject a discount at any level if the justification is missing, and
the pricing system blocks quotes without the justification field.
Discount approvals are logged with the quote code (QT-####) and are
visible to finance and the sales VP. The monthly pricing review
(second Wednesday) reviews the discount log: total discount spend,
average discount by product, and the discount-to-win-rate ratio.

## Discounts and Compensation

Discounts affect commission under the Sales Commission Plan: commission
is calculated on the invoiced ACV, so a discount reduces the
commission base. There is no commission floor for discounted deals,
and there is no special rate for them. A deal with a discount above
20% is reviewed by the commission administrator when the commission
is calculated, to confirm the discount was approved; an unapproved
discount voids the commission for that deal until the approval is
repaired. Discounts do not change the clawback rules: a refunded or
cancelled deal is clawed back per the commission plan's 90-day rule,
at the discounted value.

## Discounts and Refunds

A discounted deal that is refunded is refunded at the amount paid,
per the Refund Policy: annual plans within 14 calendar days of the
invoice, monthly plans within 7 days. The discount does not reset
the refund window and does not change the refund amount calculation.
A customer who cancels a discounted deal outside the window and
renegotiates is repriced at list, and the new quote needs its own
discount approval. Discount approvals are contract records: they are
retained with the quote and the contract per the Data Retention
Policy (seven years after the contract ends).

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Proposal and Quote Process governs how quotes are built and
issued, and the discount is attached at the quote stage. The Contract
Review and Approval Policy governs the contract thresholds (legal
review at $100,000 ACV and above); a discount approval and a contract
approval are separate chains, and both must be complete before
signature. The Invoicing and Payment Terms Policy enforces the
approved discount at billing, and an invoice with an unapproved
discount is rejected. The Partner Program Policy governs partner
pricing, which is outside this policy. The Sales Commission Plan
uses the discounted ACV as the commission base.

title: Enterprise Deal Desk Playbook
sourceName: Northwind Sales Enterprise Deal Desk Playbook
body:
# Enterprise Deal Desk Playbook

## What the Deal Desk Does

The Deal Desk sits between Sales and Finance to ensure every enterprise
agreement reflects our terms, pricing, and risk posture. We are the
gatekeepers of revenue quality, not speed. Our job is to approve
quotes, validate discounts, screen non-standard terms before legal sees
them, and hand off complete order forms to Onboarding. We do not close
deals; we make sure closed deals are safe to book. Every agreement that
crosses our desk will be executed against, and we want it to be written
so carefully that disputes are rare and our margin is real.

When to involve the Deal Desk depends on size and complexity. Any
opportunity above $100k ACV requires our review before quoting.
Discount approval flows through us for anything above our approver's
limit. Non-standard payment terms, liability caps, security exceptions,
data residency requirements, custom SLAs, or termination for
convenience clauses all route to Deal Desk first. If the customer asks
for something outside our standard contract, we are the first filter.
Small deals under $50k with standard terms and no exceptions can skip
the desk entirely, but the account owner must confirm in writing that
no deal modifications are planned. A deal that slips through the desk
because Sales believed it was small, then turns out to have custom
liability language, puts us at risk. So the rule is simple: if you are
unsure, ask the desk. We would rather spend 15 minutes clarifying that
a $45k deal is truly standard than miss a non-standard term that costs
us a lawsuit.

We do not write contracts or negotiate terms with customers. That is
legal's job after we approve the business shape. We do not do financial
due diligence or check credit worthiness, that is a finance function.
We are the translation layer: Sales asks "can we do X", we check policy
and risk, and we say yes, no, or "yes but Finance or Legal must sign
off first". We unblock good deals and reject bad ones quickly. We also
document why we said yes or no, so that three months from now, when the
deal is closed and a question comes up, we can point to a decision memo
and explain the logic. The desk exists partly to move deals through,
but just as much to leave a record of what we decided and why, so that
the company learns from its own history.

Our turnaround commitment is four business days for standard intake and
approval. If you submit a quote request on a Monday morning, you have
an answer by Friday close of business. For deals above $250k annual
contract value that route through our fast-track queue DD-QUEUE-2, the
commitment is two business days instead. That two-day window is real
only if your submission is complete: pricing clearly stated, all
non-standard terms listed, discount justification included, and
customer profile filled in. If we have to ask for clarification, the
clock restarts when we get it. So a deal that arrives with half the
information missing will take four days to get a first response saying
"here is what we need", then four more days once you provide it. Budget
for that timeline. A complete submission is faster. We also track our
own turnaround in a dashboard, and we report it monthly to the Sales
leadership and to Finance. If we slip, we escalate internally. But if
Sales misses our intake rules or sends half a deal, that delay is on
Sales, not on us.

Our intake rule is simple. Submit via the Deal Desk intake form at
deals.northwind.example, not email. The form captures: deal name,
customer name, customer annual revenue (to size them), opportunity ACV,
discount percentage if any, discount reason (competitive, volume, land,
multi-product), list of any non-standard terms requested, and who the
sales sponsor is. If you email a deal request, we will not look at it
until you submit the form. We do this because email gets lost, forms
ensure we have everything we need, and a paper trail helps when the CFO
asks later why we approved a $500k deal at 35% off. The form also feeds
our deal database, so we can run reports on discount trends, on which
customers are asking for which custom terms, on turnaround times, and
on the financial impact of our approvals. Email breaks that pipeline.
Use the form.

When a deal arrives incomplete, we send back a checklist of missing
items rather than a vague rejection. Sales can then gather what we
need and resubmit. Resubmission resets the clock, so if your initial
submission is missing discount justification, customer profile data, or
a list of non-standard terms, expect the intake-to-decision cycle to
take the full four business days (or two for the fast track) from the
date we receive your complete resubmission. The intent is not to punish
incomplete submissions but to ensure that our decision is based on
complete information. A decision made on partial data is often wrong,
and a wrong decision early in a deal's cycle causes rework downstream.
Completeness at intake saves time overall.

The Deal Desk also maintains a reference library of common deal scenarios
and approved exceptions that Sales can reference before submitting. If you
are asking for a term that we have approved many times before, check the
library first; the approval pathway may be faster. The library documents
precedent approvals for custom SLAs, discount exceptions, payment term
variations, and liability cap adjustments. It also tracks which customer
segments have negotiated which terms historically, so Sales can understand
what a similar customer has received in the past. This library is updated
quarterly and is the authoritative reference for "has Northwind done this
before". If your deal resembles a precedent in the library, we can often
fast-track approval because the commercial risk is already understood and
the legal risk has been vetted. If your deal is genuinely novel, expect
standard turnaround. Tracking precedent also helps Finance understand
whether a discount or term is becoming standard by customer type; if
half of our healthcare customers now get Net 45 when we used to offer
Net 30, Finance needs to know that the market is shifting.

Most deals will be approved at the Deal Desk level. Anything under
$100k with standard terms gets a yes within days. Deals from $100k to
$250k with no discount or a standard discount inside the Discount
Approval Policy's sales-manager band, and no term changes also get a
yes from us. The friction starts above $250k or with non-standard
terms. At that
point, Finance and Legal enter the loop, and timing extends. But we
never skip those gates. A $500k deal with custom liability language
that goes to contract without Finance review is the kind of mistake
that costs us money in a dispute five years later. We have seen
companies get sued on contracts nobody at the finance table had read,
and the defense was basically "we did not know we said that". We are
not that company.

The Deal Desk also owns the quote validity rule. Every quote we issue
carries the validity period set by the Proposal and Quote Process,
printed on the PDF. If the customer does not sign within that period, we
re-issue. This is not a guideline, it is a policy enforced by our
quoting system. After a quote ages beyond validity, material conditions
have changed: your price list may have, the customer's seat count may
have shifted, licensing terms may have adjusted based on our annual
update cycle. A quote older than its stated validity gets re-validated
and re-priced. Sales sometimes pushes back on this, saying the customer
verbally committed but needs three months to get a PO through their
process. Our answer is the same: re-issue the quote if it is stale. The
customer can sign it whenever they want, but we will not honor a quote
we issued in April when they come back in July. That rule exists because
selling at May prices in August is revenue risk, and because customers
who take three months to execute are often using our quote as an option,
shopping us against a competitor. Refreshing the quote flushes out the
seriousness of their intent. It also means that the customer is getting
the current list price and current discount, not a locked-in price from
months ago that may now be below our margin floor. We reset quotes not
to punish customers but to keep our own house clean.

The desk also manages escalations. Sales gets into a jam where they
promised something they should not have, or they are stuck between a
customer demand and a policy, or they need to know whether an exception
is possible. They call the desk. We listen, we think, and we either
unblock them quickly or we send them to Finance or Legal with a
specific question. We try to give Sales a yes or no within a few hours,
not days. If we need to go up to the CFO or to a lawyer, we do it the
same day. Sales should never feel like the desk is slowing down a deal
because we are overcautious. We are careful, but we are also fast.

## Building an Enterprise Quote

An enterprise quote is not a price estimate. It is a commercial
document that becomes the basis for the order form and the contract.
Every line item, every term, every price, every discount, every
milestone and every limitation must be true in the quote or the
contract will contradict it later, and that contradiction will cost
credibility and sometimes money. We build quotes to be signed, not to
be negotiated down again later. Once a customer has a quote from us,
they have a snapshot of what we are selling and what it costs.
Precision matters because the quote becomes the reference point for
every conversation that follows.

The building blocks are line items. Each line item is a product tier,
the annual cost, the seat count or unit count that tier represents, and
the term length. We have standard tiers across our three main products.
Northwind Core, our flagship SaaS platform, comes in three tiers:
Starter (up to 50 seats), Pro (51 to 250 seats), and Enterprise. Atlas,
our data integration product, comes in three tiers: Standard,
Professional, and Enterprise. Meridian, our customer portal, comes in
two tiers: Standard (up to 10 external admins) and Professional (11 to
100 external admins). Enterprises often buy across all three, so a
quote might have a line for Northwind Core at the Enterprise tier, a
line for Atlas Professional, and a line for Meridian. That mix is
common. Each product line has its own scope, its own pricing, and its
own term, but all three lines go on one quote and one order form, and
the customer gets one bill.

When you quote a customer, you use our published SKU. For Northwind
Core Enterprise at the 500-seat tier, the SKU is NW-CORE-ENT-500. For
Atlas Professional at the 100 pipeline tier, the SKU is
NW-ATLAS-PRO-100. For Meridian customer portal at the 25 external admin
tier, the SKU is NW-MER-PORT-25. These are the SKUs that appear on the
order form and on the invoice. You do not invent a new SKU for this
customer, you do not hyphenate differently, you do not add a suffix.
The SKU is the SKU. These standardized SKUs exist for a reason: when we
send the order form to Accounting, they need to know exactly what we
sold. When the customer renews, we need to know what we were selling
them before, so we can offer a renewal at the same tier or a bump. When
support configures their account, they need to know the SKU so they
provision the right seat count or admin tier. A bespoke SKU breaks all
of that. When a customer asks for a custom tier that does not fit our
standard buckets (say, Core at 375 seats when we sell 250 or 500), you
do not create a bespoke SKU. Instead, you propose the next tier up. If
they want 375 seats and the jump from 250 to 500 is too steep on price,
that is a negotiation for a deeper discount, not a new product tier. We
refuse bespoke SKUs because they create downstream confusion: billing
does not know how to true-up a custom tier, support does not know what
seats are included, renewal is a mess because the customer thinks their
tier is unique when every tier is standard. Standard tiers, standard
SKUs. That is non-negotiable. If a customer is so large or so important
that we want to make an exception, that decision comes from Dana Okafor
(CEO) or Victor Lindqvist (COO), not from Sales or the Deal Desk.

Pricing for each line item is annual, and it is list price minus
discount if any. List prices are maintained by Product and Finance and
are the single source of truth. You do not negotiate a new list price
with a customer. You negotiate a discount. If you are quoting Northwind
Core Enterprise 500 seats at $180,000 per year list, and the customer
needs $150,000 to get approval from their finance team, you offer a
16.7% discount, bringing the total to $150,000. You do not invent a new
list price that happens to be $150,000. That matters because list price
is what goes into renewal notices, price increase letters, and our
financial forecasts. Discounts are temporary. They apply to this deal,
this year. List prices are the baseline, the reference point, and the
starting line for every conversation. An ACV of $500k at a 20% discount
means the customer is paying $400k, but our forecast shows $500k, and
our discount approval process knows a $100k concession was made. That
transparency helps Finance understand our margin, and helps Sales
leadership understand when they are negotiating too hard.

Many enterprise deals have a ramp schedule. The customer signs today
but does not roll out to full seats until Month 6. Year 1 might be 30%
capacity, Year 2 might be 60%, Year 3 full. When you quote a ramp, the
quote shows the Year 1 cost, the Year 2 cost, and Year 3 cost. Each
year's cost is based on the seat tier and list price for that tier. Do
not apply a discount to each year individually and then stack
discounts. Apply the discount once to the ACV (annual contract value),
then show the ramped cost for each year. If the customer is ramping
Northwind Core Enterprise 500 from 30% to 100% over three years at a
15% discount, Year 1 is $150,000 (30% of the discounted ACV), Year 2 is
$300,000 (60% of the discounted ACV), Year 3 is $500,000 (the full
discounted ACV). The math is clean, the discount is obvious and applied
once, and when Year 3 comes and they want to renew, we know exactly
what they are paying. Ramps also align our cash collection to the
customer's deployment plan, so we are not invoicing for seats they have
not activated yet. That also reduces support burden, because the
customer cannot activate seats they have not paid for.

True-up is the correction that happens when reality does not match the
quote. A customer ramped to 30% in Year 1 but hit 50% actual usage by
Month 9. At the annual true-up, they owe the difference between what
they paid (30% of the year's cost) and what they used (50% of the
year's cost). True-up is not a penalty, it is an adjustment. It is how
we stay aligned with actual consumption. When you quote a deal with a
ramp, mention in the quote that annual true-ups will apply. The
customer should not be surprised at Year 1 renewal that they owe more
because they grew. The renewal team will reference that language, and
the conversation becomes "you used more, so you pay a bit more", not
"we are charging you for upgrades you never asked for". True-ups also
allow us to price a ramp aggressively, because we know we will capture
upside as the customer scales up. The customer benefits from a lower
Year 1 cost, and we benefit from the true-up when they exceed their
ramped allocation.

Overages are customers who exceed their licensed tier. If they bought
Northwind Core at 250 seats but have 270 seats active in November,
those 20 overage seats are billed at 150% of the per-seat cost of their
license tier. You do not force them back down to 250. You bill the
overage at the end of the month. This is in our standard terms, and it
applies unless the customer negotiates a ceiling (like, "our license
covers up to 250 seats but anything over goes on the next tier at full
price"). Overages keep customers from needing to buy a whole new tier
just to stay legal. If a customer grows from 250 to 251 seats, they do
not want to buy the 500-seat tier. They want to pay a little bit extra
for one seat. Overages are humane and they are profitable, because the
overage rate is higher than the per-seat rate of their current tier.

Multi-year deals sometimes include uplift. The customer commits to year
2 and year 3, and in exchange for that upfront commitment, you give
them a slight discount on the year 2 and 3 cost. Do not stack
multi-year uplift on top of volume discount. You give them one or the
other. A volume discount applies because they are a large customer
today. A multi-year uplift applies because they are committing to a
longer term. Both together are double-dipping and they destroy margin.
Pick the better one for the customer or offer the worse one if you are
the one asking for the longer commitment. If the customer comes to us
and says "we will sign a three-year deal if you give us a better
price", that is multi-year uplift, and we can offer it. If the customer
comes to us because they are a $2M ACV customer and they want a volume
discount, we offer that instead. Not both. When you are structuring a
multi-year deal, be clear about which years the uplift applies to.
Usually it is year 2 and 3. Year 1 is at the negotiated price. Year 2
and 3 get the uplift, bringing the per-seat cost down slightly. That
structure keeps incentives aligned: the customer gets an upgrade reward
for committing early.

The 30-day quote validity applies to every quote we issue. Once the
quote PDF is generated and sent to the customer, it is valid for 30
calendar days from the date printed on the PDF. If a customer receives
the quote on January 5 and signs on February 10, the quote is stale,
and we will not honor it. The customer can request a refreshed quote
with today's terms. This policy is in our standard language, and
customers know it. Some will push back, saying they need more time
because their CFO is traveling or their procurement process is slow.
Our answer is still 30 days. If they want the price to stay locked
longer, that is not our problem to solve. If the customer insists they
were verbally promised a 60-day window, that is a red flag that Sales
made a promise we did not authorize. Escalate to your sales leader and
the Deal Desk immediately. We do not honor verbal price locks. A quote
is a quote, and a quote is 30 days. After 30 days, we refresh it.

## Non-Standard Terms and How to Get Them Approved

Nearly every large customer asks for something outside our standard
contract. They want Net 45 or Net 60 instead of Net 30. They want
unlimited liability or a cap that is higher than our standard 12-month
fees. They want a custom SLA that guarantees 99.99% uptime instead of
our standard 99.5%. They ask for termination for convenience so they
can cancel without cause. They ask for their data to be stored in a
specific region. They send us a 40-page security questionnaire and ask
us to remediate every finding. They want master service agreements with
addenda and exhibits. They want us to accept their template instead of
ours. These are not unusual requests. But they are not standard either,
and they do not get approved because the customer asks for them. Every
non-standard term requires explicit approval from Finance, Legal, or
both, and the approval must happen before the customer is promised
anything. A customer who believes a term is approved when it actually
still needs legal review is a customer who will be angry when we
finally get back with notes or a rejection.

Payment terms are the most common negotiation. Our standard is Net 30:
invoice on signature, payment due 30 days later. Most US customers
accept this happily. International customers often want Net 45 or Net
60, especially if they have centralized procurement or they are in
Europe and their regulatory process is slow. You can offer Net 45
without approval. It costs a bit more cash float, but not enough to
break Finance. Net 60 requires Finance (Marcus Webb, CFO, or the
Finance Operations Manager) to sign off, because holding invoices for
60 days affects our cash flow forecasts and our ability to make payroll
if we have a slow collection quarter. Anything longer than 60 days
needs the CFO personally and almost never gets approved. You do not
offer Net 90 or Net 120. If a customer asks for it, the answer is no,
or if they are a big enough deal and we have reason to believe they are
good for it, "we can offer Net 60, and we will need 50% upfront to
offset the holdback". That upfront payment protects us, because we have
half the cash in hand immediately. We do not do payment term discounts.
You do not give them a 5% reduction because they want Net 60. The
customer pays the same amount, they just pay it later. Our price is our
price; payment terms are a separate lever.

Liability caps are the second most common negotiation. Our standard
contract caps our liability at 12 months of fees paid, and excludes
liability for indirect, consequential, or incidental damages. That
12-month cap applies to everything: performance failures, security
issues, data loss, service outages. Large customers push back, saying
12 months is too low for a mission-critical system, or they want
unlimited liability for data breaches. Uncapped liability is a
non-starter. We will not agree to it. We are not big enough or well
enough insured to carry unlimited exposure for any product. A cap
higher than 12 months requires Amelia Brooks, General Counsel, or her
team to review and approve. A cap of 24 months of fees is often
acceptable if the customer is a strong negotiator, the deal is large,
and they are willing to negotiate down from a higher ask. A cap of 36
months is rarely approved without an escalation to Amelia and the CFO.
Do not offer 36 months without checking with both. Data breaches are
covered by our cyber insurance, and Priya Raman (CISO) has authority
over any language that touches data breach liability. If the customer
wants unlimited liability for data breaches, we escalate that to Priya
and Amelia together, and the answer is usually no, unless we are
acquiring a specific customer and it is a strategic imperative. The
customer does not get uncapped liability. But we might agree to a
modest uplift (say, 24 months instead of 12) if we carry cyber
insurance that covers the difference and Priya signs off on the
language.

Custom SLAs are requests to guarantee higher uptime or faster response
times than our standard support SLAs. Our standard uptime SLA is 99.5%,
which means 3.6 hours of allowed downtime per year. Our standard
support response time is 1 hour for P1 issues and 4 hours for P2. A
customer asking for 99.9% or 99.99% uptime is asking us to engineer to
a higher bar. 99.9% uptime means 52 minutes allowed per year. 99.99%
means 5 minutes allowed per year. That is possible, but it costs money
and it means Ravi Iyer (CTO) and the engineering team need to sign off
that the infrastructure can support it, and that ongoing monitoring and
escalation protocols are in place. You do not promise a custom SLA
without engineering's approval. If a customer needs higher uptime, you
route the request to Ravi with the opportunity size and timeline, and
you wait for his team to say yes or no. If yes, the SLA goes in the
contract with specific downtime windows and maintenance windows and
notice periods are the ones published in the Scheduled Maintenance
Policy, along with credits for missed targets. If no, you tell the customer we cannot deliver it,
or we can deliver it for an additional fee to offset the engineering
cost. Do not tell the customer we will "look into it" and then
disappear. Either we can do it, we cannot do it, or we can do it for
more money. Any of those is better than a vague maybe.

Security questionnaires are routine for large customers, but they are
not a Done item until Legal and Security review them. When a customer
sends you a security questionnaire, you acknowledge receipt within one
business day, you give them a timeline (typically 10 business days,
sometimes 15 for a complex form), and you route it to Priya Raman
(CISO) and the legal team. You do not answer the questionnaire
yourself. Priya's team reviews it, flags any questions that ask for
things we do not have (like, FIPS 140-2 compliance if we do not have
it), and pushes back on unreasonable demands (like, "we need a
dedicated instance just for us" or "we need you to store backups in our
data center"). Once Priya approves the responses, Legal reviews it to
make sure nothing in our answers creates a new contractual obligation
we cannot meet. Then the Deal Desk sends the completed form back to the
customer. This usually takes two to three weeks, sometimes more if it
is a 60-page questionnaire from a large bank with 200 questions. Budget
for it. Do not tell the customer you will send it back "next week" if
you know Priya will need 10 days. Give them a realistic timeline.

Termination for convenience is a clause that says the customer can
cancel at any time for any reason, without cause, and without penalty.
Our standard contract is 12-month term with auto-renewal, and a 90-day
notice requirement to prevent renewal. The customer has to stay for 12
months. If they want to leave early, they are in breach. Termination
for convenience flips that: they can leave whenever they want,
sometimes on 30 days notice, sometimes immediately. We rarely agree to
this, because it kills the revenue certainty of a 12-month contract.
You can close a $500k deal at list price with termination for
convenience, and the customer can cancel in Month 2 and leave you with
$500k of expected revenue that never shows up. If the customer insists
on it, the price goes up 20-25% to offset the risk that they will
cancel early. If you want to offer termination for convenience, flag it
with Marcus Webb (CFO) and Amelia Brooks (General Counsel) before you
propose it to the customer. That is not a deal desk decision; it is a
business decision above us. If Finance says yes and wants to price for
the risk, we run the numbers and we approve it. If Finance says no, we
go back and tell the customer no.

Data residency and localization requests are increasing, because
customers have regulatory or contractual obligations to keep data in a
specific region. We run workloads in the US, EU, and APAC regions, with
compliance certifications for most of them. If a customer wants all
their data in the EU and we have EU infrastructure, that is easy. We
note it in the order form and hand it to Onboarding. If the customer
wants data in a region we do not serve (like, India, or mainland
China), that is not easy. It may be possible, but it requires
infrastructure decisions and potentially additional cost to set up new
facilities or partner with a regional vendor. You do not promise data
residency we do not have. Route it to Victor Lindqvist (COO) or Ravi
Iyer (CTO) to figure out feasibility and cost. If we can do it, we
charge for it. If we cannot do it, we say no. Some customers will walk
away. That is OK. Better to lose a deal than to promise data residency
we cannot deliver and then scramble when they ask us to prove it during
onboarding.

The sequencing for non-standard term approval is strict: Deal Desk
first, Finance second, Legal third. You route the request to Deal Desk
(that is you), we screen it, we check policy, and we flag what needs
Finance and Legal input. Then the request goes to Finance (Marcus Webb
or the Finance Operations Manager). Finance validates the commercial
shape: does the discount make sense for the customer size, does the
payment term affect our cash flow forecast, does the deal pencil
against the cost of goods sold, does the margin meet our floor. Then it
goes to Legal (Amelia Brooks or her team), and Legal validates the
contract language, the liability terms, the regulatory compliance, the
dispute resolution language, and the overall risk posture. You do not
send a non-standard term request to Legal before Finance approves. You
do not tell the customer a term is approved before Legal signs off. The
sequence is Deal Desk, Finance, Legal. That order exists because
Finance can kill a deal on commercial grounds (say, the discount is too
steep for the margin we need), and if Finance kills it, Legal never
sees it, and we save everyone time. And Legal should be the last gate
because a term that Finance approved might still be legally risky or
expose us to a new type of claim.

The cardinal rule is this: no term is promised to the customer before
it is approved. You do not tell the customer "we will give you Net 60",
"we will cap liability at 24 months", or "we will guarantee 99.9%
uptime" until Finance and Legal have signed off in writing. If the
customer asks in a call and you are not 100% sure, you say "that is a
good question, and I will check with our finance and legal teams and
get back to you by Thursday". You do not say "yes, I think we can do
that". Customers remember yes. They forget "I will check". If you say
yes and then have to come back three weeks later and say "we actually
cannot do that", the deal stalls, trust erodes, and the customer starts
comparing us to a competitor who already said yes. Slow is better than
wrong. It is also better for the customer: they would rather hear "that
is complex, let us get back to you" than get excited about a term that
we cannot deliver.

## Handoff to Onboarding

Once the order form is countersigned by the customer and the CEO (for
deals over $1M) or the Finance team (for deals $250k to $1M), or the
sales leader (for deals under $250k), the Deal Desk closes the approval
and hands the deal to Onboarding. Onboarding is Victor Lindqvist (COO)
and his team. They own the customer kickoff, the implementation
timeline, the success metrics, and the handoff to Support. They get a
handoff document that includes everything Onboarding and Finance need
to deliver on the deal. This is not an email. This is a structured
handoff form filled out in our deal management system, and both the
Deal Desk and Sales sign it. The handoff is the transfer of
accountability from Sales to Delivery. Once Onboarding receives it and
reviews it, they own the customer success.

The handoff includes the deal name, customer name, deal ACV, the
effective date of the contract (when the customer begins paying), the
term length (usually 12 months, sometimes 24 or 36), the renewal date
(when we send a renewal notice, usually 90 days before contract end),
and the auto-renewal setting (yes, always yes unless the customer
specifically negotiated no auto-renewal). It includes every line item
and SKU from the quote, the seat count or unit count for each, and any
ramps or true-up provisions. It includes the discount, the discount
reason (competitive, land, multi-product, volume), and the dollar
amount of the discount so Accounting knows revenue is recognized at the
discounted price, not list. It includes the customer's billing contact
and technical contact, and the preferred language for support
communications if it is not English.

It includes any non-standard term, every single one: Net 45 instead of
Net 30, unlimited liability for data breaches, custom SLA with 99.9%
uptime guarantee, data residency in the EU, termination for convenience
with 30-day notice, anything that deviates from standard. It includes
the Security Questionnaire approval status and any conditions (like,
SOC 2 attestation required by Month 3, or data retention must be 90
days). It includes the names and emails of the deal sponsor (Sales),
the finance approver, the legal approver, and the customer's main
contact. It includes any custom integrations that were promised, any
professional services, any training, any pilot period, and the timeline
for each. If the customer is piloting for 30 days before going live,
that goes in the handoff. If the customer is getting a free month of
service while they migrate data, that goes in the handoff.

It also includes the customer's industry, their size, their use case,
and their success criteria. This is context for Onboarding, so that the
implementation team understands what winning looks like for this
customer. If the customer is a financial services firm and they are
using Northwind Core to automate compliance reporting, Onboarding needs
to know that. If the customer is a healthcare company and data privacy
is their make-or-break concern, Onboarding needs to know that. This
context helps Onboarding tailor their onboarding approach and helps
Support understand what the customer cares about most.

The kickoff timing is critical. Onboarding should not learn about a
deal from the order form showing up in their email inbox. They should
hear about it at least one week before the contract is signed. The deal
sponsor (your Sales contact) emails the Deal Desk and Onboarding
together with a note saying "this deal is approaching signature,
kickoff scheduled for August 15". That email warns Onboarding that they
are about to get an inbound deal and gives them time to check calendar,
allocate resources, and reach out to the customer to schedule a kickoff
call. A good Sales contact will loop Onboarding in much earlier, at the
proposal stage, so they can give input on feasibility or timeline.
Onboarding's SLA is a kickoff call within five business days of the
signed order form. If the order form comes to them cold with no
warning, they will miss that SLA and the customer will be frustrated.
So Sales tells us, we tell Onboarding, Onboarding plans. The day the
order form is signed, it goes to Finance first, then to the Deal Desk,
and the Deal Desk sends the handoff form to Onboarding within 24 hours.

The commitments recorded in the handoff are everything Onboarding and
the delivery team are promising to the customer. If we quoted the
customer a data migration from their old system, with a specific
timeline and the customer's data ready on Day 1, and a support engineer
assigned as a primary contact, those are all commitments. The delivery
team needs to know them before they start. If the quote promised custom
integrations with the customer's warehouse system, someone in
Onboarding or Professional Services needs to be assigned to that
project before kickoff. If the quote said "your Meridian implementation
will be complete by June 30", that date goes in the handoff, and the
project manager budgets to that date. If the quote promised a training
program for 50 end users, that goes in the handoff and Finance approves
the cost. The customer expects it, and if Onboarding does not know it
was promised, they will not budget resources for it, and the customer
will feel abandoned.

We do not hand off surprises. If the contract says the customer gets a
custom SLA with a guaranteed response time of 30 minutes for P1 issues,
Onboarding needs to know that because Support (Nadia Petrov, VP
Customer Support) will need to staff to that level and may need to
escalate how fast they respond on P1 for this account. If the contract
says the customer can terminate for convenience with 30 days notice,
the delivery team needs to know that this is a month-to-month deal, not
a 12-month commitment, and they should not be planning a 12-month
onboarding roadmap with a big implementation that takes six months to
pay back. If the contract says data must be stored in the EU,
Onboarding needs to know that the customer's environments are
non-standard and require special provisioning. If the customer paid at
a higher tier but negotiated a lower seat count, Onboarding needs to
know the seat count, not the tier. If the customer gets a discount on
Year 2 and Year 3 pending a milestone (like, "discount applies if you
achieve 80% adoption"), that goes in the handoff. You capture all of
that in the handoff form, and Onboarding reads it before they call the
customer for the first time. That is the deal desk's last job: make
sure the people who deliver the deal are not blindsided by a promise we
made to close it.

The handoff review is not a rubber stamp. Onboarding's project manager
reviews the handoff and either confirms receipt with no questions, or
escalates back to the Deal Desk with feasibility concerns before the
kickoff call. If Onboarding says "we cannot deliver the custom integration
in 30 days; it will take 60", the Deal Desk must escalate that back to
Sales and the customer immediately so that expectations can be reset and
the contract can be amended if needed. A handoff that says "let's try it
anyway" is a recipe for customer disappointment and a failed onboarding.
Onboarding's role is to say early if something is not feasible, not to
discover it six weeks into implementation.

The Deal Desk also flags any deals where terms conflict or where unspoken
dependencies exist between the quote, the contract, and the legal terms.
For example, if the quote promises implementation support but the contract
says implementation is out of scope, that conflict gets surfaced in the
handoff so the customer and Sales can clarify what was really promised.
If the customer negotiated a discount contingent on Year 2 adoption metrics,
but nobody has defined what those metrics are, the handoff notes the missing
definition and flags it for Sales to resolve with the customer before
Onboarding starts work. These conflicts are caught at handoff time, not
discovered months later when the customer asks "when does our Year 2 discount
kick in" and nobody can agree on whether they hit the milestone.

After the handoff is reviewed and Onboarding confirms receipt without
escalation, the deal is in their world. Finance starts billing setup and
invoicing. Support gets a ticket to provision the account and configure
the customer's seat count or admin tier. The project manager starts
building the implementation timeline based on the customer's availability
and the commitments we made. If there is a ramp, the project manager knows
when the customer reaches each milestone and budgets the expansion work.
If there is a custom integration, the engineering team gets assigned and
the schedule starts ticking. None of this happens on its own. It happens
because the handoff form was clear about what was promised and who is
responsible.

That is the deal desk's job: approve the terms, validate the pricing,
screen the risk, and hand off a complete picture to the people who will
execute. Every deal that rolls through the desk should be one that
Finance and Onboarding are ready to deliver. If we hand off a deal and
Onboarding says "we cannot do that", the deal is at risk. If Finance
sees the terms after signature and says "we should not have approved
this", the deal is at risk. We catch all of that before signature. We
are the guardrail, and we take that seriously.

title: Partner Program Policy
body:
# Partner Program Policy

## Purpose

The partner program covers companies that resell, implement, or
integrate Northwind products: resellers, implementation partners,
and technology partners. This policy defines how partners are
onboarded, how partner deals are priced, and how partners are paid.
It is owned by sales and shared with finance, which runs the partner
payments. The program is separate from the Referral Program (which
pays employees a flat $2,000 per customer) and separate from the
employee recruiting referral. Questions go to partners@northwind.example.
Partner agreements are contracts under the Contract Review and
Approval Policy and are signed with codes in the format PT-####.

## Partner Types and Onboarding

There are three partner types. Resellers: sell Northwind products to
end customers under the partner pricing model. Implementation
partners: deliver implementations and training for customers (their
services are billed by the partner, not by Northwind). Technology
partners: build integrations under the API and Integration
Standards. Onboarding requires: a signed partner agreement, a
completed partner application with references, and (for resellers)
a minimum commitment of $50,000 in annual bookings after the first
year. Onboarding is completed within 30 business days of the
application, and partners are reviewed annually: resellers must
maintain the minimum commitment, and technology partners must pass
the integration review.

## Partner Pricing

Reseller deals use partner pricing, which is separate from the
direct discount tiers in the Discount Approval Policy: the partner
price is 80% of list ACV for the first year and 85% for renewals,
set in the partner agreement. The partner invoices the end customer
at list price or higher, and the margin belongs to the partner.
Partner pricing cannot be combined with direct discounts: a deal is
either direct or partner, never both, and this is enforced at
billing. Deal registration: a reseller registers a deal in the
partner portal before the first customer meeting to protect their
margin; unregistered deals are direct deals. The registration window
is 90 days, renewable once.

## Partner Commissions and Payouts

Partners earn a recurring commission of 10% of partner-sourced ACV,
paid quarterly. The commission applies to the invoiced ACV of
registered partner deals: 10% of the annual invoice for the first
year, and 10% of renewal invoices while the customer remains active
and the partner agreement is current. Payouts are made quarterly,
within 30 days of the quarter end, by bank transfer, with a
commission statement showing the invoices and the calculation.
Commissions are paid on paid invoices only, per the Invoicing and
Payment Terms Policy. A partner deal that is refunded under the
Refund Policy claws back the commission on the next payout, under
the same refund windows (14 calendar days for annual plans).

## Implementation and Technology Partners

Implementation partners bill the customer directly for their
services; Northwind does not pay implementation commissions. The
partner's implementation work follows the Customer Onboarding
Checklist's milestones, and the CSM coordinates with the partner.
Technology partners build to the API and Integration Standards, and
their integrations are reviewed by engineering before listing in
the partner directory. Technology partners do not earn commission;
their benefit is the directory listing and the co-marketing terms
in the agreement. A technology partner that resells (rare, and only
with a reseller addendum) moves to reseller rules for the resold
deals.

## Partner Lifecycle

Partner agreements run 12 months with automatic renewal, per the
Contract Review and Approval Policy's standard terms. Partners can
be terminated: for breach (with a 30-day cure period), for falling
below the reseller minimum commitment at the annual review, or for
violating the API standards. Termination ends deal registration
rights, and registered deals in progress are honored for 60 days
after termination. Partner records, agreements, and commission
statements are retained for seven years under the Data Retention
Policy. The partner program is reviewed quarterly by the sales VP
and the CFO: partner-sourced revenue, commission spend, and
registration conversion.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Discount Approval Policy governs direct deals; partner pricing
is set in this policy and the partner agreement. The Referral
Program pays employees, not partners, and a deal cannot be both a
referral deal and a partner deal. The Sales Commission Plan does
not pay commission to reps on partner-sourced deals. The Contract
Review and Approval Policy governs partner agreements (the partner
agreement is a contract under its thresholds). The API and
Integration Standards govern technology partner integrations. The
Invoicing and Payment Terms Policy governs partner invoices, which
follow Net 30 like direct deals. The Refund Policy governs refunds
on partner deals, which claw back commissions on the next payout.

title: Proposal and Quote Process
sourceName: Northwind Sales Proposal and Quote Process
body:
# Proposal and Quote Process

## Purpose

This process governs how Northwind Systems builds, prices, and
issues proposals and quotes. It is owned by sales and is shared with
finance, which validates quotes at billing time. Every quote gets a
code in the format QT-####, and every order references its quote.
The process applies to new business, renewals, and expansion. The
pricing source of truth is the price list in the pricing system,
maintained by finance; sales does not set prices, it applies the
list and the approved discounts from the Discount Approval Policy.
Questions go to the sales operations team.

## Quote Structure

A quote contains: the customer, the products and quantities, the
term (annual or monthly), the list price, the discount (with its
approval code), the services (setup fees and professional services
days), the payment terms, and the quote validity. Quotes are built in
the pricing system, which applies the price list automatically and
blocks invalid combinations (for example, a discount without an
approval, or partner pricing on a direct quote). Setup fees are fixed
at $2,500 for Core, $1,500 for Atlas, and $1,000 for Meridian, and
are not discountable. Professional services days are quoted at the
published daily rate and are discounted under the same tiers as
products.

## Quote Validity

Quotes are valid for 30 days from the issue date. After 30 days, the
quote expires and a new quote must be issued with the current price
list; the pricing system marks expired quotes automatically. A
customer who accepts an expired quote is re-quoted, and the
re-quote can be at a different price if the list changed. The
validity period is written on the quote, and sales cannot extend a
quote's validity manually; an extension requires the sales manager's
approval and is limited to 15 additional days. Quotes for annual
plans are valid for the term quoted; a customer who signs after the
validity period but before re-quoting has no price guarantee.

## Approval Chain

Quotes require approval before issue: the sales manager approves
quotes up to $100,000 ACV, the sales VP approves quotes from
$100,000 to $250,000, and the CFO approves quotes above $250,000.
These thresholds mirror the contract thresholds in the Contract
Review and Approval Policy, and the two chains run in parallel: a
quote above $100,000 also flags the contract for legal review. The
discount approval (Discount Approval Policy) is attached to the
quote before the quote approval; the quote approval checks that the
discount is approved, and the billing system re-checks at
invoicing. A quote cannot be issued with a pending discount or a
pending approval.

## From Quote to Order

When the customer accepts, the acceptance is recorded in the pricing
system, and the order is created with the quote reference. The
contract is then executed under the Contract Review and Approval
Policy, and the customer is onboarded under the Customer Onboarding
Checklist. The first invoice is generated at contract start under
the Invoicing and Payment Terms Policy, using the quote's prices and
terms; an invoice that does not match its quote is rejected by
billing. Changes after acceptance (add-ons, term changes) are new
quotes. Cancellations after acceptance follow the Refund Policy:
annual plans can request a refund within 14 calendar days of the
invoice, monthly plans within 7 days.

## Renewals and Expansion

Renewals are quoted 90 days before the renewal date, and the renewal
quote follows the same process: new quote code, current price list,
new discount approval (prior approvals do not carry over), and the
same validity period. The contract auto-renews under the standard
terms, but the price is set by the renewal quote: an unsigned
renewal quote at a higher price is billed at the higher price after
the renewal date, with a 15-day notice to the customer. Expansion
(add-ons) is quoted at list price with its own discount approval,
per the Discount Approval Policy's rules. Renewal quotes above
$250,000 trigger the contract review chain like new business.

## Quote Records

Quotes are retained in the pricing system with their QT-#### codes,
including expired and declined quotes. Quote records are contract
records under the Data Retention Policy: seven years after the
contract ends, or seven years from the quote date for quotes that
never became contracts. The quote-to-close rate and the average
discount are reported monthly to the sales VP and feed the pricing
review in the Discount Approval Policy. The April and October SOC 2
audits sample quote approvals as part of the billing controls.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Discount Approval Policy sets the discount tiers that quotes
apply. The Contract Review and Approval Policy sets the contract
thresholds that quotes above $100,000 flag. The Invoicing and
Payment Terms Policy bills from the quote. The Partner Program
Policy sets partner pricing for partner deals, which use partner
quotes with the partner price model. The Refund Policy governs
cancellations after acceptance. The Territory and Account Assignment
Policy determines who owns the quote and the deal.

title: Referral Program
body:
# Referral Program

## Purpose

The referral program pays Northwind employees for introducing new
customers. It is separate from the employee recruiting referral
bonus (which pays $1,000 for a new hire, under the Recruiting and
Interview Policy) and separate from the Partner Program (which pays
partners a recurring commission). This program is for employees
referring customers. It is owned by sales, and questions go to
referrals@northwind.example. The payout is a flat $2,000 per new
customer, and the program is open to all employees except: sales
roles (who are paid commission instead), the CEO, and employees who
work on the account being referred.

## How Referrals Work

An employee refers a prospect by submitting the referral form in the
referral portal before the prospect's first meeting with sales. The
form captures the prospect's company and the referrer's details, and
it creates a referral code in the format RFR-####. A referral is
valid only if submitted before the first sales meeting: referrals
submitted after the prospect is already in the pipeline are
rejected. The referrer does not participate in the sales process;
the account team runs the deal, and the referrer is not the
customer's point of contact. Referrals of current customers, of
companies already in negotiation, or of the referrer's own employer
are not eligible.

## Payout Amount and Timing

The payout is $2,000 per new customer, paid after the customer's
first invoice is paid in full. For annual plans, the first invoice
is the annual invoice, paid under Net 30 terms, so the payout
typically lands 30 to 45 days after the contract start. For monthly
plans, the payout is paid after the second monthly invoice is paid,
to confirm the customer is active. The payout is made in the next
payroll run after the trigger is confirmed by finance, and it is
taxed as ordinary income. If the customer's first invoice is
refunded under the Refund Policy (14 calendar days for annual
plans), the payout is recovered from the next paycheck.

## Eligibility Limits

An employee can refer up to 10 customers per calendar year. There is
no limit on the total payout an employee can earn within that cap.
Referrals from the same company are one customer: a second referral
from a company that already subscribed does not earn a second
payout. Referrals of government entities and public sector accounts
require the legal team's review before the referral is accepted,
because of procurement rules; the review takes up to 10 business
days. Employees who join the sales team during the year lose
referral eligibility on their first day in a sales role, and any
pending referral payouts are paid out under the rules in place when
the referral was submitted.

## Referral Tracking

The referral portal tracks the referral from submission to payout:
submitted, qualified (first meeting held), won, and paid. The
referrer can see the status in the portal, but not the deal value
or the customer's details beyond the company name. Referral records
are kept for seven years under the Data Retention Policy. The
referral program is reported quarterly to the sales VP: referrals
submitted, conversion rate, and total payouts. The program budget
is part of the sales budget in the Budget Planning and Forecasting
cycle, planned at $40,000 per year by default.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Recruiting and Interview Policy's referral bonus ($1,000 for
hires) is a different program with a different payout, and the two
are not interchangeable. The Partner Program Policy pays partners
10% recurring commission on partner-sourced ACV, which is different
from the flat $2,000 referral payout, and a deal cannot be both a
referral deal and a partner deal. The Discount Approval Policy
applies to the referred customer's deal like any other deal: the
referral payout is not affected by the discount. The Commission
Plan does not pay commission on referred deals to the account rep
beyond the normal deal commission; the referral payout is paid to
the referrer on top. The Refund Policy governs refunds that
trigger payout recovery.

title: Territory and Account Assignment
sourceName: Northwind Sales Territory and Account Assignment
body:
# Territory and Account Assignment

## Purpose

This policy defines how accounts and territories are assigned to the
Northwind sales team. It is owned by sales and is shared only within
sales because it contains the territory structure. Assignment
determines who owns a deal, which drives commission under the Sales
Commission Plan: commission follows the account owner on the closing
date. The policy is administered by sales operations, and assignment
disputes are resolved by the sales VP. The territory model is
reviewed annually in January, and changes take effect on February 1.

## Territory Model

Territories are defined by region and segment. The regions are:
Americas (Austin-led), EMEA (London-led), and APAC (Singapore-led).
The segments are: enterprise (annual value above $100,000), mid-market
($25,000 to $100,000), and small business (below $25,000). Each
account is assigned to exactly one territory: one region and one
segment. Account executives own territories (a region-segment
combination, or a sub-region for enterprise), and account managers
own the renewals and expansion for existing accounts within the same
territory. New territories are created only in the January review,
except for hires mid-year, which split an existing territory.

## Assignment Rules

New accounts are assigned by sales operations within five business
days of the first inbound lead or meeting request. Assignment follows:
the lead source's region and segment, then the current load of the
territory owners (balanced by account count and pipeline value).
Inbound leads are assigned to the owning territory's account
executive; outbound leads are owned by the rep who sourced them and
are assigned to that rep's territory when the account is created. An
account can change territory only: when the segment changes (an
account growing above $100,000 moves to enterprise at the next
quarterly review), when the annual review reshapes territories, or
when the sales VP approves a transfer. Account changes are logged
with the account code (AC-####).

## Account Transfers

A transfer moves an account from one owner to another. Transfers
happen for: segment changes (with the quarterly review), territory
reshaping (February 1), manager direction (with the sales VP's
approval), and departures (the exiting rep's accounts are
reassigned within 5 business days of the departure date, per the
Termination and Offboarding Policy). Commission on transferred
accounts: the rep who closed the deal keeps the commission, and the
new owner earns commission on renewals and expansion from the
transfer date. A transfer in progress does not change the closing
owner: commission follows the account owner on the closing date, and
sales operations records the owner of record for every quote
(QT-####).

## Disputes

Assignment disputes (two reps claiming the same account, or a rep
claiming an account assigned elsewhere) are filed with sales
operations within 10 business days of the assignment or the
dispute event. Sales operations investigates the lead history and
the first-meeting record: the account belongs to the rep who logged
the first qualified meeting, unless the account was assigned by an
inbound lead, in which case the assignment wins. The sales VP
decides unresolved disputes within 5 business days. Disputes that
involve commission are resolved by the commission administrator
under the Sales Commission Plan, using the owner of record on the
closing date. Dispute decisions are final and are logged.

## Records and Reporting

The account assignment log records: the account, the owner, the
territory, the assignment date, and every change with its reason.
The log is the source of truth for commission and for pipeline
reporting. The territory review in January produces the territory
map for the year, and the map is distributed to the sales team on
February 1. Assignment records are retained for seven years under
the Data Retention Policy, and the quarterly segment review report
(accounts moving between segments) goes to the sales VP and
finance. The territory map feeds the sales forecast in the Budget
Planning and Forecasting cycle.

## Relationship to Other Policies

The Sales Commission Plan uses the owner of record from this
policy's log to pay commission, and its clawback rules apply to
transferred accounts. The Proposal and Quote Process assigns quotes
to the account owner. The Recruiting and Interview Policy covers
hires that create new territories. The Termination and Offboarding
Policy triggers the reassignment of departing reps' accounts. The
Partner Program Policy governs partner-sourced accounts, which are
assigned to a partner manager, not to the territory account
executive.
